At night - more in the grim lands, many more under a blood moon - and underground at any hour, things come that are not animals or monsters. Each has its own way of hunting: the tall one at the edge of the trees that is gone when you look straight at it, the statue that only moves when you don't, the thing that is a little closer every time you turn around.
Your heart beats faster when one is near. Some whisper. A few will take things from you. When dawn finds them, they're gone.

Far out over deep water, by chance alone (likelier in the Kraken Deep and in a storm), the sea goes quiet, rumbles, boils - and the Kraken comes up. It fights with its arms: one rears up over you (a ring of foam marks where it will fall: get out of it) and comes down like a falling tree; swimming, you're grabbed and dragged under (hammer SPACE or hurt it to break free); in a boat, arms coil round the hull and squeeze. Its arms can be cut as well as its body. Flee far enough, or into the shallows, and it sinks away; kill it and it leaves the Kraken Lord's Mantle and a leviathan's rib.

Every biome's monsters can come as a boss (a great one of its kind, with a health bar and its own drops). Castles, crypts, dragon roosts, colosseums, dungeons and pyramids keep one each, and the lords of the Abyss sit on thrones far below.

Spoilers: the whole story is below.

The story begins at Briar's Rest and runs through eight acts: the census and the convoy; the toll fort, the bandits, the landing tower and the harbour at Reedwake; Saint Orra's Isle and its inspector; the Underworld and its pens; the Last Gaol and the creditor on his throne; the wyvern of the Needles; Crownreach in the sky, its service quarter and its people; and the King in his castle.

Everything the story uses is in the world from the first day: its people at their posts, its garrisons, its bosses in their arenas. You can go anywhere and fight anything; the story will deal with you when it reaches you. Its papers and carvings can be read early, and those objectives will already be done.

Spoilers: what each circle does to you.
Every demon and soul of the circles wakes as a real creature when you come near. Kill every demon keeping a group of the damned and the group is free, and follows you.

A Hellmouth opens the land into the Vestibule. Every circle below is sealed off from the next by solid rock, and the only way down is that circle's own Hellmouth, in a keep whose gate opens to the key the circle's Warden keeps.

How the game works: surviving, fighting, crafting, magic, and more.
What to do on your first day.
Food, water, temperature, stamina and rest.
What each kind of armour is good for.
How rare things are, and what rarity does.
What the world's peaceful folk make of you, and what they do about it.

You wake on an old road with nothing. There are lights up ahead: Briar's Rest, a settlement built into an abandoned royal waystation. Its people take you in, and teach you what you need: what can be gathered by hand, how to make a flint knife and then an axe, how to make fire and boil water, how to hunt and cook, how to carry light, how to fight, and how to rest.
Follow the chapter shown at the top right of the screen; L opens the journal. Talk to people with E. Everything you can see can be picked up with E or broken apart by hitting it.
Keep your food and water up, stay warm (or cool), and sleep somewhere safe. The night is far more dangerous than the day.

Food and water fall over time, faster when you work hard. At zero you begin to starve or dehydrate. Raw meat and dirty water can make you sick: cook meat on a fire, and boil water from a lake or river before drinking it (the biome's page says whether its water is safe).

Your body temperature follows the air: hot deserts and frozen wastes will kill you without the right clothes. Fur and padded armour keep you warm; cloth and silk keep you cool (see Armour classes). A fire warms you, and so does shelter.

Stamina goes on sprinting, rolling, jumping and swinging, and comes back when you rest. Sleep in a bed to pass the night and to set where you wake if you die. Dying leaves a grave with everything you carried.

Every blow is a real thing in the world: it only lands if the blade, the head or the fist actually touches the body it's swung at, and creatures' teeth and claws must really reach you. Swing at what's in front of you, and watch their reach.

A blow has a wind-up, a fast strike (the only part that can hit) and a recovery. Hold the attack to charge a heavier blow. Weapons run through a combination of blows while you keep attacking; a sword or spear thrusts when you lunge in at a sprint.
Tap Shift to roll through a blow. Interrupt a creature's wind-up with a hit and it staggers. Heavy weapons (greatswords, hammers, maces, axes) stagger hardest and knock things back.
Armour blocks a share of the damage you take: armour / (armour + 18). Elemental resistances cut that element further. Critical blows do double damage.
Creatures see and hear you: crouch, keep to cover and the dark, and wear quiet armour to get close unseen (see Stealth).

Creatures have a field of view, a sight range (longer for hunters, shorter in the dark) and hearing. Moving fast and sprinting make noise; crouching and standing still make little. Cover, tall grass and darkness hide you; a torch in your hand at night gives you away.
Leather and cloth armour, and some great pieces, add Stealth: you make less noise and are harder to see. Plate makes no difference to how you're heard - but it does slow you.
Tab opens the crafting book beside your pack: everything you know how to make, in the order you'll need it, with what it takes and where. Click a recipe and press CRAFT.

Some things are made by hand; most need a station - a campfire, a crafting table, a tanning rack, a loom, a furnace, an anvil, an alchemy table, an altar or the dragon forge. Craft the station, place it, then look at it and press [E]: its own menu opens, with only what is made there. Nothing at a station is instant - meat hangs on the spit and browns, ore glows in the furnace, a blade lies on the anvil - and when it is done you look at the station and press [E] again to take it. Food left on a fire too long burns.
Weapons and armour are made in nine materials: wood (or cloth), stone (or hide), bone, bronze, iron, obsidian, crystal, dragonbone and voidforged. Each is better than the last.

Spells are cast from a staff, wand or tome that carries them. Left mouse casts the spell in hand; R switches between the spells it carries; the greatest spells must be held to charge. Each cast costs mana, which comes back over time; a better staff holds more.

There are six tiers of spell, from Novice sparks to the Cataclysm spells that break the land. Spell power - from robes, tomes and great pieces - makes every spell stronger. Wands cast faster and weaker; tomes stronger.
Mages, monsters and bosses use magic too, and the most powerful bosses keep one cataclysm for late in the fight.

Every piece of armour is of a class, read from what it's called and what it's made of. The class sets how much armour it gives and what else comes with it, scaled by how much of you the piece covers (body armour the most, then leggings, helm, boots, gloves, cloak).
Plate: the most armour, and slower (helms, cuirasses, plate, sabatons, gauntlets, cuisses of metal).
Mail and Scale: good armour, a little weight (coifs, hauberks, chausses; scale mail, lamellar, brigandine).
Leather: lighter armour; quicker and quieter (jerkins, vests, masks, boots, gloves, leggings).
Padded: warm and quiet (gambesons, tunics, trousers). Cloth: cool and the quietest (hoods, cowls, sandals, wraps, cloaks).

Robe: almost no armour, but more spell power and a little healing (robes, skirts, shrouds). Fur: built for the cold (mitts, mantles, pelt cloaks). Finery: luck and a little magic (crowns, circlets, diadems, capes).
Gear comes in eight rarities: Common (white), Uncommon (green), Rare (blue), Very Rare (teal), Epic (purple), Legendary (orange), Exotic (pink) and Unique (every colour).

From one roll with no luck: one find in five is Uncommon, one in twenty Rare, one in eighty Very Rare, one in four hundred Epic, one in two thousand Legendary, one in ten thousand Exotic, one in fifty thousand Unique. Loot luck, bosses and dangerous places help, the rarest least.

Rarity adds to a thing's numbers and gives it more affixes - and it shows: a Rare piece has a jewel set in it, Very Rare glowing runes, Epic motes of light about it, Legendary a ring of light and a crest of flame, Exotic shards of itself floating free, Unique a halo of every colour.

Under your equipment in the inventory is a row of vanity slots, one for each place you wear something. What's in a vanity slot is how you look there, over whatever you actually wear - so you can keep your best armour on and look however you like.

Cosmetic items (horns, hats, wings, regalia) go there by themselves when you right-click them. Shift-right-click puts any piece of armour there instead of wearing it. Your figure in the inventory, and you in third person (V), show how you look.

The world is full of real animals - hundreds of species, each in the lands that suit it - and the monsters of each biome, people of many trades and factions, and the horrors that come out of the dark.

Creatures fight each other: wolves run down deer, lions and hyenas feud, mongooses go for cobras, raptors take rabbits, orcas take seals. Predators hunt what's smaller; the apex hunters run off lesser ones; anything that would kill you will kill people too. Bandits, cultists, the undead, the Iron Legion and the rogue mages feud with each other; guards and soldiers fight back while townsfolk run. Struck creatures turn on whatever struck them, and their kin join in. Predators stop to eat their kills.
The bestiary (J) records every species you've seen.

Your renown runs from -100 to 100 and is shown on the inventory screen (Tab), beside your health. Word travels: every town knows it. It falls when you strike (-4) or kill (-15; a guard -20) townsfolk or wanderers - anyone peaceful - and when you take from a home while its people watch (-2). It rises when you kill bandits, cultists and the risen dead (+1.5), keep monsters off the folk (+1), defend someone in need (+3), finish a side quest (+6), slay a terror of the land (+5) or one of the great enemies (+10). A bad name fades slowly - a point every ten minutes - if you keep your hands clean.

Monster (-60 and below): guards, hunters and sellswords cut you down on sight; everyone else runs. Outlaw (-60 to -30): exiled - a town's guards order you out, and come for you if you stay or push past them; folk flee from you, and doors in town are barred. Distrusted (-30 to -10): no greetings; people back away; guards tell you to watch yourself.

Stranger (-10 to 10): nobody minds you. Liked (10 to 30): warm greetings; the guards nod. Honored (30 to 60): people come up to you with gifts - a flower, bread, something from their garden or their shop - and ask you home to share their table. Hero (60 and up): all that, and the guards, hunters and sellswords fight beside you when something comes for you.

A price on your head: every crime adds to your bounty (an assault 20 coins, a theft 15, a murder 100, a guard's 200), shown under your renown. WANTED posters with your own face on them go up round every town you come near (and by Briar's Rest's gate). From 250 coins, parties of bounty hunters - hard, well-armed people who know your face - set out after you from somewhere behind you: the bigger the price, the more often, the more of them and the stronger. Read a poster with E; carry enough coin and you can pay the bounty off there. Once your renown is back above -10 the bounty lapses, slowly.
Console: /rep shows your standing; /rep N sets it. /bounty shows the price on your head; /bounty N sets it; /bounty hunt sends hunters now.

Feed a tameable creature what it eats and it may follow you: up to three companions at once (the Companions screen shows them). Passive, skittish and neutral creatures can be tamed, and wolves and cats of any kind, and some of the wild things (dire wolves, ironshells, hollow stags, lantern wisps, thornbacks, glass scuttlers). People, bosses, horrors, demons, swimmers and anything very large can't.

Two things can be ridden. The storm drake, the lesser winged kind, roosts at the foot of Mount Hessaril: feed it meat three times and it's yours to ride. Close over a mountain's faces it rides the wind rising off them, and it'll carry you up as high as the Needles' shoulder - no higher. The high wyvern hunts a circuit over the Needles' spires: drop onto its back from above and hold on through its struggle, and it will carry you anywhere - over the summits, and even up to Crownreach.

Wild high wyverns are found nowhere but round the summits of the Worldspine's mountains, swimming wide loops far above the cloud. Stand in the open on the snow near a summit and one will drop on you out of the sun - and the fall is the worse of it. They let you be when you're riding one of their own.

Each biome has its own weather: rain, thunderstorms, hail, fog, blizzards, sandstorms, tornadoes and hurricanes. Lightning strikes the high ground; tornadoes lift what they reach; blizzards freeze. Shelter from the worst of it.
Every biome's page says what weather it gets; every kind of weather has its own page, below.

"Taken from the collar of the gluttons' watchdog. All three heads still wake when it rings."

"'Dearest Lamp. You are the only light that turns toward me every night.' It was a long winter."

Keeper's Unquenched Lamp is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Still lit. The keeper died in a storm; the lamp never got the message."
Swearing Parrot Feather is a beast parts in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Hold it to your ear and it curses like a bosun. Some words are new. Some you heard from your mother."
Dropped by parrot, bird (3% a kill)
Wizard's Odd Sock is a components in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Embroidered with stars that move. Its partner is in another century and not looking."
Ghost's Unposted Letter is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Sealed, addressed, never sent. The ghost would very much like you to post it."
Overdue Invoice of Sins is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"From the Inferno's Registry of Sins, fourth notice. Interest compounds per lie. Your name is spelled right."
Firefly Promise Jar is a provisions in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Three fireflies and a promise to let them go in the morning. You won't. They know."
Wyrmling's Milk Tooth is a beast parts in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Lost in its first fire. Put it under your pillow and wake up singed, but richer."
Dropped by drake, wyrm (5% a kill)
Golem's Love Poem is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Chiselled one word a year: 'YOU. ARE. A. NICE. ROCK.' He was not finished."
Tiny Crown for a Toad is a treasures in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Taken off a toad who flatly refused to say where he got it."
Dropped by frog, toad (4% a kill)
Skeleton's Spare Rib is a beast parts in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Kept in a pocket for emergencies. Skeletons have no pockets. It is complicated."
Wheel of Moon Cheese is a provisions in Thornveil. It can be eaten or drunk (right mouse button with it in hand).
"Fell out of the sky into a crater. Tastes of cold milk and distance."
Compass That Points Home is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"It points to wherever you last felt safe. For some owners, it only spins."
Cheater's Iron Dice is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Always six. Their owner was killed for it by men who also, somehow, rolled six."
Shell That Remembers the Sea is a beast parts in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Hold it to your ear: the sea is in there, and a man asking where his boat went."
Giggling Puffball is a plants in Thornveil. It can be eaten or drunk (right mouse button with it in hand).
"Step on it and it laughs. Eat it and so do you, for an hour, at nothing."
Four-Century Overdue Book is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Due back four hundred years ago. The fine has grown teeth and opinions."
Wanted Poster of You is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"An excellent likeness. The reward is frankly insulting."
Dropped by bandit, knight (5% a kill)
Petrified Sandwich is a provisions in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Ham and stone. A lunch forgotten under the old trees, now a monument to good intentions."
Jar of Bottled Thunderclap is a provisions in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Opened once at a wedding. The bride's hair has stood on end for eleven years."
Snowglobe of a Lost Village is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Shake it gently and the tiny villagers look up. One waves. They're just friendly."
Diary That Writes Back is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Write 'dear diary' and it replies 'what now'. It has strong views on your choices."
Ever-Warm Cocoa Mug is a provisions in Thornveil. It can be eaten or drunk (right mouse button with it in hand).
"It refills when you're sad. Owners of this mug are rarely seen without it."
Kraken's Lost Earring is a treasures in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Big enough to wear as a belt. It slipped off in a fight with a frigate, and the kraken still sulks."
Caught on a line in deep water
Lich's Grocery List is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"'Newt eyes (fresh). Grave soil. Milk.' Even the deathless forget the milk."
Dropped by undead, skeleton (3% a kill)
Bell That Rings for Liars is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Silent in honest company. Owners report that it is never silent."
Egg That Hatches Yesterday is a the catch in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"It was laid tomorrow and hatched yesterday. Today it's just complicated."
Dragon's Hoard Inventory is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Every coin named and loved. One is listed 'missing (thief, eat on sight)'. It's the one in your purse."
Lantern of Captured Sunset is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Caught by a shepherd who wanted the evening to last. It has, for three hundred years."
Hourglass of Five Minutes More is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Turn it and five extra minutes appear. Nobody has ever spent them on anything but sleep."
Imp's Rude Noise Box is a components in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Open it and it makes a rude noise in the demon tongue. Devils find it hilarious every single time."
Siren's Tangled Comb is a treasures in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"One green hair is caught in it, and it hums when wet. Do not hum back."
Caught on a line in sea water
Ribcage Xylophone is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Tuned to C major by a patient necromancer. The original owner still taps along."
Witchhouse Gingerbread Shingle is a provisions in Thornveil. It can be eaten or drunk (right mouse button with it in hand).
"Pried off a cottage roof. The witch has filed a complaint, and a curse."
Sulking Fairy in a Jar is a provisions in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"She lights the room but won't speak to you. Let her out and she speaks, mostly in swears."
Greedy Compass is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"It points to the nearest gold. Usually that's your own teeth."
Pebble From the Bottom is a minerals in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Picked up from where the world stops. It is heavier on the way back."
Storm Roc Wishbone is a beast parts in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Pull it with a friend. The loser is struck by lightning, which is a kind of wish."
Dropped by roc, thunderbird (5% a kill)
Mask of an Unmade Face is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Wear it and your face makes an expression nobody has made before. Mirrors refuse to show it."
Bottled First Snowfall is a potions and reagents in Thornveil. It can be eaten or drunk (right mouse button with it in hand).
"A century of first snows, corked. It smells of woodsmoke from a house you never lived in."
Clockwork Nightingale is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"It sings the song of whoever wound it last. Its current song belonged to a dead king. It's sad."
A Cat's Spare Life is a potions and reagents in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Cats get nine. This one was never used; the cat was far too smug to die."
Dropped by cat, lynx (1% a kill)
Jarred Piece of Night is a provisions in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Scooped from between two stars. A small moon orbits the lid."
Dragon's Beloved Teddy is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Scorched, chewed and loved for a thousand years. The dragon is coming for it. You know this."
Box of Every Lost Sock is a components in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Where they all go. Yours is in here. So is a king's, a giant's, and one that is still warm."
Mirror That Compliments is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"It says only kind things, and only true ones. With some owners it has been very quiet."
Hellhound's Squeaky Skull is a beast parts in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"It squeaks in the voice of the man it used to be. The hound adores it."
Bonfire Taffy is a provisions in Thornveil. It can be eaten or drunk (right mouse button with it in hand).
"Handed out in the Inferno to keep the damned busy. It works. Your molars disagree."

Mat(Ext(1741)).t: Coin That Lands on Its Edge
s: Coin That Lands on Its Edge is a treasures in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Flip it for any decision and it refuses to choose. The wisest coin in Thornveil."
Pet Raincloud is a treasures in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Follows you like a duckling. Waters your crops. Rains on your enemies' picnics."
Candle That Burns Cold is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Its flame frosts the wick instead of melting it. Moths visit it and leave colder, and wiser."
Drowned Bard's Lute is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Waterlogged and still in tune. When it plays, fish rise to the surface and weep."
Caught on a line in deep water
Treaty of Crabs and Gulls is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"A peace accord, signed in claw and beak. The gulls broke it within the hour."
Unmelting Snowcone is a provisions in Thornveil. It can be eaten or drunk (right mouse button with it in hand).
"Scraped from the coldest summit. Drop it in a forge and the forge gets a headache."
Hourglass of Borrowed Time is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Every grain is an hour someone didn't get to live. Turn it over and they feel slightly better."
Bottled Laughter of a God is a potions and reagents in Thornveil. It can be eaten or drunk (right mouse button with it in hand).
"A god found something funny once, and a monk caught it in a bottle. Nobody knows the joke."
Map of Your Last Step is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Your route is marked in red and ends in an X. You keep folding it so the X is hidden."
Next Year's Music Box is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"It plays the song everyone will be humming next year. Bards would kill for it. Several have."
Leviathan Calf's Rattle is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Coral, the size of a cart. Shake it and somewhere a mother leviathan looks up."
Caught on a line in deep water
Phoenix Egg Omelette is a provisions in Thornveil. It can be eaten or drunk (right mouse button with it in hand).
"The egg hatched in the pan. You ate around the bird. It's fine. It came back."
Contract Signed by Nobody is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"A soul-sale with the name scratched out. The devil is still looking for whoever outwitted him."
The Wish Not Spent is a treasures in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"A child threw it in a well and forgot to wish. It has been waiting, glowing, very patiently."
Caught on a line in fresh water
Fool King's Bell Crown is a treasures in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Every bell rings a different lie. The fool who wore it ruled forty years in peace."
Lantern of Lost Things is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Its light shows only what was lost: keys, socks, years, the names of old dogs."
Ghost Fleet in a Bottle is a provisions in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"A whole drowned armada sails in circles inside the glass. On stormy nights the cork rattles."
Caught on a line in deep water
Snowglobe of Thornveil is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"It is the whole world, tiny. Shaking it is unwise. Somebody did, last winter. You may remember."
Dice Carved From a Moon is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Whatever you roll, the sky shows that many moons that night."
Egg of Tomorrow's Dawn is a the catch in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Crack it and the sun comes up. At midnight. Underground. The cockerels are furious."
Tin Knight's Wind-Up Heart is a beast parts in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Still ticking, still in love with a lady of the court three centuries dead. It won't stop."
Dropped by golem, knight (1% a kill)
Last Sweet of the Damned is a provisions in Thornveil. It can be eaten or drunk (right mouse button with it in hand).
"Given to each soul at the Vestibule, for courage. Nobody ever finishes it. You will."
The Lighthouse's Reply is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"Written in light on salt paper: 'I always knew. I turned for you too.' The sea took its time."
Caught on a line in sea water

Mat(Ext(1764)).t: The Duck at the End of Everything
s: The Duck at the End of Everything is a curios in Thornveil. It is a treasure, worth having for its own sake.
"It floats on the nothing under the world. Something vast has been bathing with it for an age."

Sword (Sword, Blade, Saber, Longsword, Falchion, Rapier, Scimitar, Broadsword, Gladius) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. The all-rounder: quick enough, long enough, a combination of cuts and a thrust when you lunge in at a sprint.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Ingot of the Drowned King Longsword
Axe (Axe, Hatchet, Cleaver, Waraxe, Battleaxe, Bearded Axe) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. A woodsman's tool that is also a weapon. It fells trees the fastest of anything, and its chop is heavy.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Ingot of the Drowned King Battleaxe
Pickaxe (Pickaxe, Mattock, Pick) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. The miner's tool: it breaks stone and digs out ore. A poor weapon, but it will do.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Ingot of the Drowned King Pickaxe
Mace (Mace, Maul, Morningstar, Club, Hammer, Warhammer) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. A heavy head on a short haft. Slow, and it hits hard; blows from it stagger.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Ingot of the Drowned King Morningstar
Spear (Spear, Lance, Glaive, Pike, Trident, Halberd, Partisan) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. Held in both hands, the front one guiding: the longest reach of the melee weapons, thrusting only.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Ingot of the Drowned King Spear
Stormcall, Spear of the Tenth Sky
Dagger (Dagger, Knife, Shiv, Stiletto, Fang, Dirk, Kris) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. The fastest blade, and the shortest. Stabs and flicks, quick enough to interrupt most things.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Ingot of the Drowned King Dagger
Greatsword (Greatsword, Claymore, Zweihander, Flamberge, Executioner) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. Two hands, a wide sweep and an overhead cleave. Slow, terrible when it lands.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Ingot of the Drowned King Greatsword
Scythe (Scythe, Reaper, Sickle, War Scythe) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. A long curved blade on a long snath: wide sweeps that catch more than one thing.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Bow (Bow, Longbow, Shortbow, Recurve, Warbow, Hornbow) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. Hold to draw, let go to loose. The longer you hold, the harder and further it shoots. Arrows are used up.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Staff (Staff, Wand, Rod, Scepter, Crook) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. Carries spells. Left mouse casts the spell in hand, R switches spell, hold to charge the great ones. Uses mana.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Star of the Ninth Circle Scepter

Headgear (Helm, Hood, Crown, Mask, Cowl, Great Helm, Horned Helm, Bascinet, Sallet, Barbute, Kettle Hat, Skullcap, Coif, Circlet, Diadem) is a kind of armour in Thornveil. Worn on the head. Helms of metal are heavy and strong; hoods and circlets light.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Every piece of armour is of a class, read from what it's called and what it's made of. See
Ingot of the Drowned King Helm
Halo of the Dawn That Waited

Body Armour (Cuirass, Tunic, Mail, Plate, Vest, Hauberk, Brigandine, Robe, Breastplate, Scale Mail, Lamellar, Jerkin, Gambeson) is a kind of armour in Thornveil. Body armour: the largest share of your protection. What it's made like decides what it's good for.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Every piece of armour is of a class, read from what it's called and what it's made of. See
Ingot of the Drowned King Cuirass
Boots (Boots, Greaves, Treads, Sabatons, Sandals, Wraps, Striders, Shoes) is a kind of armour in Thornveil. On the feet. Light boots are quiet and quick; sabatons and greaves strong.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Every piece of armour is of a class, read from what it's called and what it's made of. See
Ingot of the Drowned King Greaves

Charm (Amulet, Talisman, Ring, Totem, Sigil, Pendant, Locket, Idol, Medallion, Rune) is a kind of armour in Thornveil. An amulet, ring, talisman or idol, worn for what it gives (it has no armour of its own).
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Star of the Ninth Circle Amulet
Star of the Ninth Circle Ring
Katana (Katana, Tachi, Uchigatana, Wakizashi, Odachi) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. A long single curved edge: fast, with a better chance than most of a critical blow. Wielded like a sword.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Ingot of the Drowned King Katana
Thrusting Sword (Estoc, Epee, Smallsword, Tuck, Needle) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. Long, stiff and narrow, made for the thrust: the highest chance of a critical blow of any weapon.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Twinblade (Twinblade, Double Blade, Spinblade, Moonglaive) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. A blade at each end of a central grip: wielded in both hands in fast spinning sweeps.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).

Great Hammer (Great Hammer, Sledge, Earthbreaker, Pounder, Great Club) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. The heaviest thing you can swing. Very slow; it hits harder and throws things further than anything else.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Ingot of the Drowned King Great Hammer
Flail (Flail, Chain Mace, Threshing Flail, Ball and Chain) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. A spiked head on a chain: heavy, with a good deal of knockback. Wielded like a mace.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Halberd (Halberd, Poleaxe, Bardiche, Bill, Voulge) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. Axe, spike and hook on a long shaft: the reach of a spear and blows nearly as heavy as an axe's.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Ingot of the Drowned King Halberd
Claws (Claws, Bagh Nakh, Cestus, Knuckles, Talons) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. Worn on the fist: the fastest blows of all, short reach, and each one drinks a little life.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Sickle (Sickle, Kama, Hook Blade, Khopesh) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. A short hooked blade: quick, light, wielded like a dagger.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Whip (Whip, Lash, Scourge, Chain Whip) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. A long lash: the longest reach of any melee weapon, light blows.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Crossbow (Crossbow, Arbalest, Repeater, Hand Crossbow) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. Spanned, a bolt in the groove: slower to shoot than a bow, and it hits much harder.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Greatbow (Greatbow, Siege Bow, Titan Bow) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. A bow taller than a man: the furthest and hardest shot of any bow.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Wand (Wand, Baton, Focus, Sceptre) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. A slender rod for casting: spells come quicker from it, a little weaker. Uses mana.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Star of the Ninth Circle Focus
Tome (Tome, Grimoire, Codex, Spellbook, Psalter) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. A book of spells, held open: spells cast from it are stronger. Uses mana.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Gloves (Gloves, Gauntlets, Bracers, Mitts, Handwraps) is a kind of armour in Thornveil. On the hands: gauntlets of steel, leather gloves, fur mitts, bracers, handwraps.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Every piece of armour is of a class, read from what it's called and what it's made of. See
Ingot of the Drowned King Gauntlets
Cloak (Cloak, Cape, Mantle, Shroud, Pelt Cloak) is a kind of armour in Thornveil. On the back: cloaks, capes, mantles, shrouds. Little armour, but warmth, speed or stealth.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Every piece of armour is of a class, read from what it's called and what it's made of. See
Leggings (Leggings, Cuisses, Chausses, Trousers, Skirt) is a kind of armour in Thornveil. On the legs: plate cuisses, mail chausses, leather leggings, trousers or a long skirt.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Every piece of armour is of a class, read from what it's called and what it's made of. See
Ingot of the Drowned King Cuisses
Shovel (Shovel, Spade, Trowel, Scoop, Excavator) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. Digs soil and sand in big scoops; poor on rock.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).
Builder's Hammer (Mallet, Claw Hammer, Builder's Hammer, Gavel, Forge Hammer) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. A builder's hammer: breaks anything built, and knocks apart stone.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).

Fishing Rod (Fishing Pole, Rod, Reel Rod, Fly Rod, Deep Rod) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. Right-click to cast into water; right-click again when the float dips to land a fish - or now and then a lost trinket or a costume piece. Rarer rods bite sooner and bring up better things.
Each of these has its own shape. Which one you find is chance; what it is made of, its rarity and its rolls decide the rest.
What it's made of sets its numbers (rarity adds to them: see Rarity).

Grappling Hook (Grappling Hook, Hookshot, Chain Hook, Claw Line) is a kind of weapon in Thornveil. A grappling hook: right-click a cliff or a ceiling to be hauled up to it; jump or right-click to let go.

Sevraakh is one of the great enemies of the story. It waits in its place from the first day, whether or not the story has brought you to it: fly there in god mode and it is there to fight.
Saint Orra's Isle, the inspection chamber beneath the warden's tower

What lives inside Magister Severin. In the story you must first break the three ward stations that shield him; met early, he stands in his chamber already shed of his human shape. He marks the floor and pulls you toward the marks. Keep moving.
Kill it before the story reaches it and it stays dead; when the story's own fight with it comes, it comes back for that.
Patrol Captain is one of the great enemies of the story. It waits in its place from the first day, whether or not the story has brought you to it: fly there in god mode and it is there to fight.
The Cinder March of the Underworld, on his patrol route
A Warlord leading a patrol of Gaol knights, with a prisoner on a chain behind him. Kill the patrol first if you can; the captain hits hard but slowly.
Kill it before the story reaches it and it stays dead; when the story's own fight with it comes, it comes back for that.

Kill it before the story reaches it and it stays dead; when the story's own fight with it comes, it comes back for that.
Registrar is one of the great enemies of the story. It waits in its place from the first day, whether or not the story has brought you to it: fly there in god mode and it is there to fight.
The Archive of the Last Gaol, by the pool of records
It writes back what is cut: it repairs itself and inscribes marks on the floor. Hit it hard and often, and stay off the marks.
Kill it before the story reaches it and it stays dead; when the story's own fight with it comes, it comes back for that.

The Bastion spur, by the great winch
The keeper of the chain that holds the Gaol's causeway. Heavy, armoured and with a great reach.
Kill it before the story reaches it and it stays dead; when the story's own fight with it comes, it comes back for that.
Satan is one of the great enemies of the story. It waits in its place from the first day, whether or not the story has brought you to it: fly there in god mode and it is there to fight.
The Court of the Last Gaol, on the throne in the keep

The creditor himself. Three phases: at two-thirds and one-third of his health he changes how he fights, and at the end he pins himself to his throne behind a shield that comes and goes. Roll through his blows (tap Shift) and break his stance.
Kill it before the story reaches it and it stays dead; when the story's own fight with it comes, it comes back for that.
Captain Teren Voss is one of the great enemies of the story. It waits in its place from the first day, whether or not the story has brought you to it: fly there in god mode and it is there to fight.
The descent dock of the service quarter of Crownreach
Captain of the quarter: a knight with a shield he blocks with from the front. Get round him. In the story he may yield, or even come over to you.
Kill it before the story reaches it and it stays dead; when the story's own fight with it comes, it comes back for that.

Commander Aubrecht Sall is one of the great enemies of the story. It waits in its place from the first day, whether or not the story has brought you to it: fly there in god mode and it is there to fight.
The leads of the castle roof
The commander of the royal guard, with four of the guard about him. Pull them apart.
Kill it before the story reaches it and it stays dead; when the story's own fight with it comes, it comes back for that.
King Aldren is one of the great enemies of the story. It waits in its place from the first day, whether or not the story has brought you to it: fly there in god mode and it is there to fight.
The Crown Room at the top of the castle

Aldren the Preserver. He blocks blows from the front, and in his second phase a covenant holds him above the last third of his health until its four anchor-lines are broken. Every blow on him is weaker until they are.
Kill it before the story reaches it and it stays dead; when the story's own fight with it comes, it comes back for that.

Tempest is an trinket in Thornveil.

Wildheart is an trinket in Thornveil.

Anvilborn is an trinket in Thornveil.

Hasteweave is an trinket in Thornveil.

Miasma is an trinket in Thornveil.

Titanhand is a trinket in Thornveil.

Barrowking's is a trinket in Thornveil.

Zephyr is a trinket in Thornveil.

Oracle's is a trinket in Thornveil.

Thousand-Thorn is a trinket in Thornveil.

Sunforged is a trinket in Thornveil.

Firstfire Hands of the First Fire
Received is a side quest, asked by Wenna Dray (a farmer's widow). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Wenna Dray: You came up the road. Did you pass a cage on it? Iron bars, a blue board on the side with a gold mark.
Wenna Dray: It came through in the spring with my boy in it. Corin. Fifteen. They left me a paper with a seal, saying he went of his own free will.
Wenna Dray: He couldn't write his own name, and there it is on the paper, signed. Somebody signed it for him.
Wenna Dray: The drovers say the cage broke an axle on the hill road and the soldiers left it there. I can't walk that far any more. If there's anything of his on it...
Wenna Dray: Up past the split oak, where the road doubles back. Thank you. Whatever's there - I'd rather know.
1. Find the census cage abandoned on the hill road
2. Take Corin's tag back to Wenna Dray
3. Show Nessa Vale the tag from the cage
Find the census cage abandoned on the hill road
"Linen tags are still tied along the bars, a dozen of them, stitched in one small, neat hand: a name, a place, a number, and a word."
"The thread of RECEIVED is older than the rest. Sun-faded. It was stitched first, and the name added after."
You: Received. They had the word ready before they'd been to the door.
Take Corin's tag back to Wenna Dray
Wenna Dray: ...That's his name. That's how they spell it.
Wenna Dray: Received. Like a sack of meal.
You: There are other tags on that cage. The same hand stitched all of them, and the same word, before the names.
Wenna Dray: Then there are other women in other kitchens with the same paper as me.
Wenna Dray: You've a look about you, like you know someone who'd want to see this. Take it to them. I'll keep the paper with the seal. I want to remember how neat it was.
Show Nessa Vale the tag from the cage
You: A tag off a census cage on the hill road. A boy called Corin Dray. Look at the stitching.
They: That's the hand on Edrin's receipt. The same loops on the R. I've looked at that receipt every night for a year.
They: RECEIVED, before the name. Somebody sits in a warm room and stitches that word a hundred times before breakfast, and then they go and find the names to put after it.
They: Keep doing this. Every one of these is somebody's Edrin.
Wenna Dray: I put the tag in the prayer-book with his father's lock of hair. Received. I can say it now without wanting to break something.
Wenna Dray: Come by at harvest. There's no one to eat the apples.
: That tag you brought me. I keep thinking of someone stitching RECEIVED a hundred times before breakfast.
: Wenna Dray's boy. I delivered him. Don't tell me any more about it, or I'll want to go and get him myself.
The Spoiled Tithe is a side quest, asked by Abel Saye (miller). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Abel Saye: Things fall out of the sky round here. You'll have seen. Mostly what you'd expect from a city - broken pots, bones, slops.
Abel Saye: Last week a crate came down whole. I saw it go into the far field. Before I could get a cart to it, the Mallory lot from the old quarry had been at it.
Abel Saye: I want to know what was in it. A crate that size, falling from up there - I've a feeling I know, and I want to be wrong.
Abel Saye: The far field, past the stone wall. And watch for the Mallorys - they don't share.
1. Find the crate that fell into Saye's far field
2. Deal with Grub Mallory, who took the sacks
3. Tell Abel Saye what was in the crate
Find the crate that fell into Saye's far field
"A crate of white-painted wood, split along one side. Inside, grain sacks, black with rot - good grain once, soaked and left to spoil."
"Every sack has the same stamp in blue: SAYE'S MILL - TITHE OF THE ROAD - YEAR 262. Under it, in a different ink: SURPLUS. TO THE CHUTES."
"Half the sacks are gone. Drag marks lead off toward the old quarry."
You: He sent them his grain. They didn't need it, so they threw it away - down here, onto the people who grew it.
Tell Abel Saye what was in the crate
You: Your grain. Your stamp on every sack. 'Surplus. To the chutes.'
Abel Saye: ...Two winters we ate turnips so the tithe crates would be full when the bell went. Two winters.
Abel Saye: And they had too much of it. They had so much they threw it over the side and let it rot on the field it came from.
Abel Saye: I'd thank you for the Mallorys, but I don't much care about the Mallorys. Here. Take this. I can't look at it today.
Abel Saye: I've stopped looking up. It's a choice, and I'm making it.
Abel Saye: If you see anything else come down with my stamp on it, burn it. I mean that.
: Saye's grain came back down rotten? I mended the wheels on the carts that took it up. I'd like those days back.
: They throw food away up there. Real food. I told Pip and she didn't believe me.
The Founder's Mark is a side quest, asked by Ida Brannock (bellfounder). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Ida Brannock: I cast bells. Cast them, tuned them, hung them in half the chapels from here to the coast. My mother did it before me.
Ida Brannock: Sixty years ago the crown bought every bell we could make, all one weight, all one note. Census bells. My mother cast four hundred of them.
Ida Brannock: There's one hanging on a frame up on the shoulder of the hill, by the old drovers' track. It rings at night. There's no wind up there to do it, and nobody hangs on the rope.
Ida Brannock: I want to know if it's one of hers. Every bell from our yard has the mark cast in the lip. Would you climb up and look?
You: I'll look at the bell.
Ida Brannock: Good. Look on the inside of the lip, low down. A ring with a line through it.
1. Find the bell on the drovers' track and look for the founder's mark
2. Bring Ida Brannock 3 iron ingots for a clapper-stop
Find the bell on the drovers' track and look for the founder's mark
"A bronze bell, waist-high, on a frame of black timber. Cold to touch, though the sun's been on it all day."
"Low on the inside of the lip: a ring with a line through it, cast clean. And beside it, cut in afterwards with a chisel - the royal census mark."
"Something has been scratched into the bronze below that, over and over, too fine and regular to be a tool slipping. It's the same mark that was cut into a gateway older than the kingdom."
You: It's hers. And someone else has signed it since.
Bring Ida Brannock 3 iron ingots for a clapper-stop
Ida Brannock: A ring with a line through it. My mother's.
Ida Brannock: And the crown's mark on top, and that other thing under it. I know that one too. It's on the old census rolls, on the seals. I always thought it was decoration.
Ida Brannock: Iron, good. I can't unring it. But I can cast a stop for the clapper, so whatever's pulling on it below has nothing to pull.
Ida Brannock: If someone asks why the bell on the hill went quiet, tell them the founder's daughter did it. It was always our bell first.
Ida Brannock: It's quiet up there now. I sleep through. I'd forgotten what that was like.
Ida Brannock: Four hundred of them. I'm going to have to find the rest, aren't I.
: A bell-stop, cast from my iron? Good use for it. I heard one of those bells in the Last Vein. I'd pay to have that one quiet too.
A Name from the Isle is a side quest, asked by Maud Fenner (net-mender). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Maud Fenner: Word came along the coast that somebody opened the cells on Saint Orra's. That the beam over the spire went dark.
Maud Fenner: My sister went over on the census boat eleven years ago. Lise Fenner. They said she was a servant now, in the city. They said she was lucky.

Maud Fenner: Some of the ones who came back off the isle are living rough in the dunes, past the point. They won't come into the village. I don't blame them. I can't go - they'd look at me and see the boat.
Maud Fenner: Would you ask them? Lise Fenner. Dark hair, a burn on her hand from the tar pot. Somebody might remember.
Maud Fenner: Past the point, where the dunes go grey. Take bread - they won't have any.
1. Ask the people back from Saint Orra's about Lise Fenner
2. Tell Maud Fenner what became of her sister
Ask the people back from Saint Orra's about Lise Fenner
They: You came over on the ebb. I saw you. You were the one in the cells with the key.
You: I'm looking for someone. Lise Fenner. A burn on her hand from tar.
They: Lise. Tar-hand Lise, we called her. She sang when the warders weren't on the stair.
They: She was in my intake. Eleven years ago. They didn't send her up to any city. Nobody went up. They sorted us - this lot to the Archive, that lot to the Furnace, the strong ones to the Bastion.
They: She went down the Black Stair in the first month. I'm sorry. I'd tell her sister myself, but I can't go near the village. I'd see the boat.
Tell Maud Fenner what became of her sister
Maud Fenner: You talked to them. I can see it.
You: Bryn Corrie remembered her. She sang when the warders weren't listening. She never went to the city. They took her down the stair under the isle.
Maud Fenner: Down. All this time I've been looking up.
Maud Fenner: Thank you. I mean that, even if it doesn't sound like it. Take this - it was hers. She'd want it used, not kept.
Maud Fenner: I've stopped mending the nets facing the city. I face the isle now. It's closer to where she is.
Maud Fenner: Bryn came into the village yesterday. Just to the well. That's further than last week.
: The ones back from the isle are living in the dunes? Tell them there's room here. Tell them nobody here will ask.

i: Petra Lunn, of the service quarter, once
s: What Fell is a side quest, asked by Petra Lunn (of the service quarter, once). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Petra Lunn: You're the one who flew. With the wizard. I was on the dock when the winch let go - I came down on the launch with the bakers.

Petra Lunn: Everything I had was in a tin box under my bunk in the Long Kitchen dormitory. My mother's letters. From down here. She wrote to me for nine years and I never knew what she was saying to me until I could read.
Petra Lunn: The whole quarter came down in pieces. Some of the dormitory roof is out on the plain - you can see the slates from the ridge. Something's living in it now.
You: I'll look for the tin.
Petra Lunn: A tin box, blue, with a bread-stamp on the lid. Be careful. It isn't only the roof that came down.
1. Clear what's nesting in the fallen dormitory roof
2. Search the fallen roof for Petra's tin
3. Bring Petra Lunn her mother's letters
Search the fallen roof for Petra's tin
"Under a sheet of white plaster, a blue tin with a baker's stamp pressed into the lid. Dented. Still shut."

"Inside: letters, dozens, folded small. Each in the same round hand. 'My Petra. The well froze. Mara Venn set my wrist for me again, I told her it was you that pushed me. The census bell rang and they took the Hollis woman. Do they let you see the sky?'"
"The last one is dated the week before the fall."
Bring Petra Lunn her mother's letters
Petra Lunn: That's it. That's the dent from when Ama dropped it down the stair.
You: She wrote about Briar's Rest. About Mara Venn.
Petra Lunn: Then she lived near there. She might still. I could walk. There's nothing above me any more to stop me walking.
Petra Lunn: Take this. I've been carrying it since the dock. It was the quarter's, and the quarter's gone, so it's mine to give.
Petra Lunn: I'm going to walk to Briar's Rest when it's warmer. Will you tell them I'm coming? Don't tell them why.
Petra Lunn: There's a whole sky up there now. Nobody told me it would be so loud with birds.
: A girl from the city asking after her mother, who wrote letters up from here? There were a few who did that. I'll ask. Quietly.
The Last Shepherd is a side quest, asked by Osric Tamm (shepherd). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Osric Tamm: Sixty-eight years old and I'm the only one minding these sheep. My sons went with the collectors. Grandsons too, last year. The receipts say they were keen.
Osric Tamm: Wolves know it. They know it's just me and a stick. Four ewes in a fortnight.
Osric Tamm: I'm not asking you to save the flock. I'm asking you to make the wolves think twice about this hill.
Osric Tamm: They come down the gully at dusk. Four of them should do it - they'll learn.
2. Tell Osric Tamm the wolves have had their lesson
Tell Osric Tamm the wolves have had their lesson
Osric Tamm: I heard it. Last night was quiet. First quiet night since the bell.
Osric Tamm: My eldest used to do that. Walk out at dusk with a bow and come back whistling.
Osric Tamm: Take a fleece. Take two. There's nobody else to wear them.
Osric Tamm: Quiet nights. I'd forgotten I liked them.
Osric Tamm: If you see a lad with my nose on him anywhere you go, you tell him his da's still on the hill.
Telling the Bees is a side quest, asked by Effie Lusk (beekeeper). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Effie Lusk: You have to tell the bees. When somebody in the house dies, you go out to the skeps and knock, and tell them. Or they take offence and go.
Effie Lusk: My Davey went with the collectors at midsummer. The paper says he wanted to. He's not dead. Is he? I didn't know what to say to them, so I said nothing.
Effie Lusk: And they've gone. All three skeps, out over the heather in one roaring morning. Nobody ever told me what you say to bees about the census.
Effie Lusk: The peat-cutter saw a swarm hanging off something on the high moor. Would you find them? And tell them. Whatever you think is true.
Effie Lusk: North, past the peat cuttings. Speak quiet. They don't like a raised voice, and they know a lie.
1. Find Effie Lusk's swarm on the high moor
2. Bring Effie Lusk 6 fibre to weave a new skep
Find Effie Lusk's swarm on the high moor
"A royal census banner on a leaning pole, the blue gone grey, the gold mark half unpicked by the weather."
"The pole has split and it's hollow inside. The swarm has gone into it - the whole length hums, and new comb shows white in the crack."
"Cut into the wood at knee height, long ago, in capitals: TOLD THEM. 249."
You: I knock three times, the way she said.
You: 'Davey Lusk went with the collectors. He didn't want to. Nobody knows where they take people. Effie wants you home.'
Bring Effie Lusk 6 fibre to weave a new skep
Effie Lusk: You told them? What did you say?
You: That he didn't want to go. That nobody knows where they take people.
Effie Lusk: ...That's more than I was told. The paper had a seal on it and less in it than that.
Effie Lusk: They'll come back to a new skep if it smells of the moor. I'll weave it tonight and carry it up at dusk.
Effie Lusk: Somebody told them in forty-nine, as well. Cut it in the pole. I'd like to know what they said.
Effie Lusk: They came back. Half of them. The half that believed you, I expect.
Effie Lusk: I tell them everything now. The census, the price of salt. They're better company than the paper.
: Telling the bees. My mother did that. Nobody's told mine about my sister. Maybe I ought to.

i: Hob Ferrin, lamplighter of the royal road
s: The Forty-First Lamp is a side quest, asked by Hob Ferrin (lamplighter of the royal road). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Hob Ferrin: Forty-one lamps on the royal road through this wood. My grandfather had the commission off the crown. Wick, oil, glass. My father after him. Then me.
Hob Ferrin: Last pay came when I was nine. I kept on. You don't let a road go dark because somebody stopped paying.
Hob Ferrin: Only I can't walk the far mile now, not with this knee. The forty-first's been dark a year.
Hob Ferrin: And it's lit again. Three nights running I've seen it from the ridge. I didn't light it. Would you go and see who did?
Hob Ferrin: Follow the posts. Count them if you like - I do, every night, in my head.
1. Find out who's lighting the forty-first lamp
2. Find whoever's been sleeping by the far lamp
3. Tell Hob Ferrin who lit his lamp
Find out who's lighting the forty-first lamp
"The forty-first lamp, on its iron post by a fallen milestone. Burning low, on tallow, not oil - somebody's fed it what they had."
"Tucked under the base, a scrap of dispatch paper with the crown's blue edge, written on the back in pencil:"
"'Sorry about your oil. I will pay when I can. I can't sit in the dark out here. I've seen what goes along this road at night.'"
You: Boot prints off between the trees. Army issue, the nails worn down.
Find whoever's been sleeping by the far lamp
They: Don't. I'm not going back. I'll go in the river first.
You: I'm not here for you. The lamplighter wants to know who's been lighting his lamp.
They: ...Oh. Him. Tell him sorry about the oil.
They: I marched a cage up this road in the spring. Escort. Seven in it, and a girl younger than my sister singing so the others wouldn't cry.
They: At the forty-first the serjeant said we'd make camp. I went into the trees to piss and kept walking. I don't know what that makes me. Not much.
They: The lamp's the one thing I've done since that I'm sure was right. Tell him I'll keep it lit, if he'll let me.
Tell Hob Ferrin who lit his lamp
You: A lad who walked away from a census escort. He sleeps by the forty-first. He says sorry about your oil.
Hob Ferrin: Sorry about the oil. Hah.
Hob Ferrin: Walked a cage up my road and then sat at the end of it in the dark with his conscience. That's a lamplighter, near enough.
Hob Ferrin: Tell him the glass wants cleaning on the inside. He'll know I mean it kindly. And you have this - it was my father's. I'll not walk the far mile again.
Hob Ferrin: Forty-one lit. First time in a year. I counted twice.
Hob Ferrin: He came by for oil. Shook like a leaf. I gave him soup. The crown owes me forty years' wages - it can owe me a deserter as well.
: A lad who walked off the escort? Good. I mended the axles on those cages. I'd have liked to walk off too.
The Ring-Heart is a side quest, asked by Gil Haddow (thatcher). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Gil Haddow: My Bettany went into the old ring on Midsummer Eve. Barefoot, in her good dress. Stepped over the caps and she was gone.
Gil Haddow: The neighbours say the census bell went that same night and the soldiers had her on the road by morning. They say it kindly. They're wrong.
Gil Haddow: It was the Fair Folk. Everyone knows the Fair Folk give you back. Seven years, and you walk out of the ring the same age you went in, with a song nobody can teach you.
Gil Haddow: You call them home with a ring-heart - the white flower dead centre of the oldest ring. Only the things that keep the rings come out at dusk. Will you?
Gil Haddow: Out past the three hawthorns. Thin out what comes at dusk and the ring's open. Don't eat anything you're offered.
1. Kill 4 of the things that keep the rings
2. Find the ring-heart in the oldest ring
Find the ring-heart in the oldest ring
"A ring of pale caps forty paces across, so old the grass inside it is a different green. Dead centre, one white flower on a stem like wire."
"Pressed into the soft ground beside it, half grown over: a boot print, hobnailed, crown issue. Then another, and another, straight across the ring and out the far side."
"A scrap of linen is caught on the caps, stitched in a small neat hand. Only the end of a word is left: ...EIVED."
You: I take the flower. I leave the scrap where it is.
Gil Haddow: You've got it. Is it white? It has to be white.
Gil Haddow: Good. Good. I'll plant it by the door, and she'll see it when she comes out, and she'll know which house.
Gil Haddow: Did you see anything else out there? Anything of hers?
Gil Haddow: Seven years, then. Six and a bit. Here - you've been in a ring and come out again, that's luck on you. My gran swore by this.
Gil Haddow: It's taken. The flower. My gran said that means she's seen it.
Gil Haddow: Six years and ten months. I've started thatching her a room.
: You let him keep the Fair Folk? ...Good. I'd have done the same, and hated myself the same.
Dead Three Times is a side quest, asked by Gammer Sallow (of the Witchwood). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Gammer Sallow: Come in, mind the cat, mind the other cat. You'll want to know why a census officer's been knocking at a dead woman's door.
Gammer Sallow: I'm dead, you see. Three times on their roll. Drowned in 222, fever in 230, a fall in 241. I wrote the letters myself each time, very sad, with a lock of goat's hair.
Gammer Sallow: They don't collect the dead. It's the one thing they're particular about.

Gammer Sallow: But there's a man going round the villages selling names to the census. A coin a head, more for the young. Lem Garrick. He's found my third grave and dug it up to show the officer it's empty. Go and see what he's left.
You: I'll look at your grave.
Gammer Sallow: Under the crooked yew, east. Don't fill it in. I'll want it again.
1. Find Gammer Sallow's third grave under the crooked yew
3. Tell Gammer Sallow about Garrick's list
Find Gammer Sallow's third grave under the crooked yew
"A grave under a crooked yew, dug open, the board pulled up. The pit is empty but for an old boot and a great many snail shells."
"The board reads: HERE LIES WINIFRED SALLOW, WHO FELL. 241. STRUCK FROM THE ROLL."
"Pinned to it with a knife, a list in a bad hand: 'Sallow - not ded - 2 coin. Pruitt boy - 3 coin. The Abney girls - 5 coin the pair. Show offiser Thursday.'"
You: He isn't only selling her. He's selling the whole valley, by the head.
Tell Gammer Sallow about Garrick's list
Gammer Sallow: I heard. The crows told me, and then the Pruitt woman told me, and she was quicker.
You: He had a list. You, the Pruitt boy, the Abney girls. He was taking it to the officer on Thursday.
Gammer Sallow: Thursday. They'd have rung the bell Friday.
Gammer Sallow: Give it here. I'll put the Pruitt boy down dead of the spotted fever - officers won't come near the spotted fever. The Abney girls I'll drown, poor lambs. Neatly. On paper.
Gammer Sallow: You'll have a cup of something before you go. No, not that one. That one's for the officer.
Gammer Sallow: Four more deaths this week. All lovely. The officer wept at one.
Gammer Sallow: If you ever need to be dead, come to me. I do a good drowning.
: She writes people dead so they can't be taken? Could she do me? I mean - if there's time.
: A man selling names at a coin a head. I'd have been slower about it.

i: Marion Brack, keeper of the White Horse
s: Scouring the Horse is a side quest, asked by Marion Brack (keeper of the White Horse). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Marion Brack: See the hill? There's a horse cut in it. White chalk under the turf, a hundred yards nose to tail. Older than the road. Older than the city, my nan said.
Marion Brack: Every seventh summer the whole village goes up and scours it - weeds out, fresh chalk rammed in - or the grass has it back in a generation.
Marion Brack: This is the seventh summer. There's me, the Tully twins and a man with one arm. Everyone else went with the bell.
Marion Brack: And something's wrong with it. Up close the lines go odd at the head. Would you climb up and look at the stone by the eye?
You: I'll climb up and look.
Marion Brack: Go up by the ear. Don't walk on the lines - it's bad luck, and it scuffs.
1. Look at the stone by the White Horse's eye
2. Bring Marion Brack 5 flint to cut the old head back
Look at the stone by the White Horse's eye
"A standing stone set in the turf at the horse's eye. Old, lichened, worn smooth - and on its face, much newer, the gold census mark cut deep."
"Under it, a plate: SURVEY OF THE CROWN. FIGURE AMENDED TO THE ROYAL MARK, YEAR 201. TO BE KEPT IN THIS FORM."
"From the eye you can see it: newer trenches, chalked a shade brighter, turning the head and mane into the census mark. The horse's own head still shows under the turf, as a line of greener grass."
You: They recut it so it reads from the sky. Sixty years the village has scoured their mark and called it the horse.
Bring Marion Brack 5 flint to cut the old head back
You: The old head's still there under the turf. The grass grows greener on it.
Marion Brack: My nan scoured that. I've scoured it eight times. We've been keeping their mark bright for them and singing the horse songs over it.
Marion Brack: Flint, good. We'll cut the old head back. The Tully twins can turf over their bit. If the crown wants it kept, the crown can come down and keep it.
Marion Brack: If anybody up there's looking, they'll see a horse. That's all I want. Somebody up there to see a horse.
Marion Brack: You can see his eye from the road again. His own eye. He looks surprised.
Marion Brack: The one-armed man cried. Said he'd scoured that mark eleven times and thought he was keeping something.
: Is there really a white horse on a hill? Can the city see it? I hope it can.

i: Imogen Hask, keeper of the blossom register
s: The Blossom Register is a side quest, asked by Imogen Hask (keeper of the blossom register). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Imogen Hask: When a child's born in the vale, we plant a cherry for them. I keep the register - which tree is whose. Seven hundred trees. My mother kept it, and hers.
Imogen Hask: If a tree blossoms early, the child's in luck. If it drops its blossom in a day, somebody takes them soup. That's what the register's for. It's a kindness, mostly.
Imogen Hask: The census officer asked to borrow it in the spring. To check his roll was right, he said. He'd send it back with the convoy.
Imogen Hask: He didn't. The convoy camped at the head of the vale before it left. Would you go and see if he left it there?
You: I'll look for your register.
Imogen Hask: The old camping ground above the falls. A green book, this thick. Every name in it is in my hand.
1. Find the convoy's camp above the falls
Find the convoy's camp above the falls
"What's left of a convoy camp: a cold fire ring, wheel ruts, a lean-to of crown canvas gone green. Under it, wrapped in oilskin, a green book."
"Imogen's register. Page after page in a round hand: a tree, a name, a year. Here and there someone has added a tick in blue ink."
"A loose sheet in the back, in a clerk's hand: 'VALE REGISTER (borrowed). 31 persons not on roll. Entered. Tags to follow. Return book with convoy - not urgent.'"
You: He didn't borrow it to check his list. He borrowed it to make his list longer.
Imogen Hask: That's it. That's my mother's binding.
Imogen Hask: Why are there ticks? I don't tick them.
You: He found thirty-one people in it who weren't on his roll. He's put them on.
Imogen Hask: I wrote them down so they'd be remembered. Every child in this vale, so nobody would ever be forgotten.
Imogen Hask: Rowan's in here. My Rowan. Is he ticked?
Imogen Hask: Go. Please. Take something - take this - I can't have anyone looking at me just now.
Imogen Hask: I've burned it. The trees will have to remember by themselves.
Imogen Hask: Some of the thirty-one have gone up into the hills. Rowan won't. He says running is what makes them come twice.
: He used her register to find them? Her kindness? I've a list of every child I've ever delivered. I'm burning it tonight.

i: Imogen Hask, keeper of the blossom register
s: Not Up is a side quest, asked by Imogen Hask (keeper of the blossom register). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Imogen Hask: You found my register. I burned it, after. It didn't help. The bell came at harvest and took twenty-six of the thirty-one. Rowan with them.
Imogen Hask: They say somebody opened the cells on Saint Orra's. That's you as well, isn't it. You've that look.

Imogen Hask: One of ours came back. Cass Orrin, the cooper's girl - her tree's the crooked one by the bridge. She's sleeping in the old orchard and she won't come into the village. She won't talk to me.
Imogen Hask: She might talk to you. I only want to know where they went. I'll not ask more than that.
Imogen Hask: The old orchard, where the trees went wild. Tell her nobody blames her for coming back.
1. Find Cass Orrin in the old orchard
2. Tell Imogen Hask where Rowan went
Find Cass Orrin in the old orchard
They: You were on the isle. I saw you on the stair with the keys. I'm not going back to the village. Don't ask me.
You: Imogen Hask wants to know where the others went. Rowan.
They: Imogen. She wrote us all in, didn't she. In her lovely book.
They: ...That's not fair. She didn't know. None of us knew.
They: They sorted us on the isle. A man with a slate. Rowan went in the first lot, down the stair under the chapel. Not up. There isn't any up. I was kept back for the kitchens.
They: I can't go home and have her look at me like I'm the lucky one. Tell her where. Tell her I'm sorry about the book.
Tell Imogen Hask where Rowan went
Imogen Hask: She talked to you.
You: Rowan went down a stair under the isle. Not to the city. Nobody from the vale went to the city.
Imogen Hask: Thirty-one trees in this vale I can't look at. And all this time I've been looking up for them.
You: She says she's sorry about the book.
Imogen Hask: She's sorry. Gods. No - I'll tell her myself. I'll take her soup. That's what the register was for.
Imogen Hask: Cass came to the bridge yesterday and stood by her tree. I didn't go out. Next time I will.
Imogen Hask: I've started a new book. Just the trees, this time. No names.

Quest(13).t: Soup at the Head of the Vale
i: Imogen Hask, keeper of the blossom register
s: Soup at the Head of the Vale is a side quest, asked by Imogen Hask (keeper of the blossom register). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Imogen Hask: Cass says people are walking up out of the ground. Out of caves, out of old mine roads, up from wherever they were kept.
Imogen Hask: A drover saw some of them camped at the head of the vale last night. Thin as rakes, he said. And something followed them up out of the dark - it's been at their fire every night.
Imogen Hask: I can't hope. I've done hoping. But I've a pot of soup and two good legs, and whatever's following them doesn't care about soup.
You: I'll go ahead of you.
Imogen Hask: Clear the way, then. I'll be ten minutes behind you with the pot.
1. Kill the thing that followed the walkers up into the vale
They: Is it dead? It's been behind us since the gate. It went for the slow ones.
You: It's dead. There's someone coming up the path with soup.
They: How long have we been gone? You can't count, down there. I thought it was years.
They: Harvest. Is my tree still standing? By the mill race. Did it blossom, while I was gone?
You: Your mother will know. She's ten minutes behind me, with a pot.
They: Mum. ...Will you stand here with me till she comes? I don't think my legs will.
Imogen Hask: He's eating. He eats like somebody's timing him.
Imogen Hask: His tree blossomed in the spring. I didn't write it down. I didn't need to.
: She walked up a hill with soup, and her son was at the top of it. Say it again. Slower.
Coldbrook's Cage is a side quest, asked by Madoc Treace (charcoal burner). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Madoc Treace: Twenty years I've burned charcoal for the crown's convoys. Braziers for the escorts, forge-coal for the wheelwrights. They pay in salt and leave me be.

Madoc Treace: There's a convoy camped at my clamps now, waiting on a burn. A cage with it. Empty. They've been asking me about the families up the valley - who's got sons, whose daughter goes to the well alone.
Madoc Treace: I've never asked what rode in the cages. I was always careful not to.
Madoc Treace: I'm asking now. It's them or me, and I'm too old to fight them and too old to keep pretending.
You: I'll deal with the escort.
Madoc Treace: There's a serjeant, Coldbrook. He's the one asks the questions. The rest of them just eat.
1. Deal with Serjeant Coldbrook's escort at the charcoal clamps
2. Search the convoy's cage by the clamps
3. Bring Madoc Treace the tags from the cage
Search the convoy's cage by the clamps
"The convoy's cage, on its wagon by the smoking clamps. Empty. On a nail inside the door, a bundle of linen tags, already stitched."
"Names from up the valley, a dozen of them, each with RECEIVED stitched first in faded thread. The last tag is newer than the rest."
You: They weren't waiting on a burn. They were waiting on him to finish it.
Bring Madoc Treace the tags from the cage
Madoc Treace: It's gone quiet down there. Is it done?
You: It's done. There were tags in the cage, stitched ready. Families up the valley. And you.
Madoc Treace: Twenty years of salt. And they'd stitched me in before I'd finished their coal.
Madoc Treace: Give them here. All of them.
Madoc Treace: ...There. In the clamp. Best charcoal I'll ever burn, that.
Madoc Treace: Take a sack of it. And this - Coldbrook won't want it, and I've had enough crown things in my hut.
Madoc Treace: The valley came down to see the clamp. Nobody said anything. They just stood in the smoke.
Madoc Treace: I'll burn for the forge at Briar's Rest now, if your smith wants it. Salt's fine.
: Treace's charcoal? I've used it for years and never thought whose it was. He wants to sell to me? Tell him yes. Tell him I know how he feels.
