The Line Through the Glass is a side quest, asked by Wren Abbott (glass-leaf gatherer). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Wren Abbott: The trees in here drop glass in autumn. Leaves of it, thin as a fingernail. We gather them for windows - there's a chapel down the coast glazed in nothing else.
Wren Abbott: Last week something came down through the canopy, very fast. It cut a line through the trees like a scythe. Glass everywhere. It sounded like the whole wood laughing.
Wren Abbott: I followed the line as far as I dared. There's something at the end of it. I think it's a person. I couldn't make myself look.
Wren Abbott: Follow the broken trees. Wrap your hands. The glass stays sharp a week after.
1. Follow the broken trees to whatever came down
2. Bring Wren Abbott 3 cloth to bury the flier in
Follow the broken trees to whatever came down
"At the end of a long gash of shattered glass trees: bones in the wreck of a harness. Canvas wings ribbed with split cane, scorched black along every edge, though nothing near them burned."
"A boy, or a small man. The bones are clean already. The glass did that."

"In an oilskin in the harness, a letter: 'Mam. They said you went up to be a servant in the city. I built these from the drawings on the old landing tower. If it works I'll be with you by supper. If it doesn't, I tried.'"
You: The ward. He got close enough to touch it.
Bring Wren Abbott 3 cloth to bury the flier in
Wren Abbott: A boy. With wings.
You: He was trying to reach his mother in the city. Something up there burned him out of the air.
Wren Abbott: We bury gatherers in cloth, so the leaves don't cut them on the way down. It's an old thing. I don't know where it's from.
Wren Abbott: I'll put him under the big tree, where they fall thickest. They'll cover him every autumn. Best-glazed boy in the world.
Wren Abbott: Keep this. It's a leaf off the line he cut. The ones that fall like that don't break.
Wren Abbott: The leaves are falling on him already. They chime when they land. I go and listen.
Wren Abbott: If there are drawings on that landing tower, somebody should scratch them off. Not that it would stop the next boy.
: He built wings from drawings? ...I'd have tried it. If it was Aunt Mara up there, I'd have tried.
White Cords is a side quest, asked by Morwen Teale (cord-weaver). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Morwen Teale: We weave the cords. You'll have seen them, if you've been near a census cage - the white silk cords the tags hang on. The crown's had them from Silkshroud since before my grandmother.
Morwen Teale: Strong, they wanted. Strong enough not to rot on a long road. We were proud of that. Our cord goes all the way up to the city, we used to say.
Morwen Teale: Now there's word along the coast that nobody in those cages went to the city. That they went to the isle, and under it.

Morwen Teale: The crown's agent comes for this year's order at the full moon. I've a mind to send him something different. I'll need silk, and the reeling-house spiders have gone wild since the reelers went with the bell.
Morwen Teale: Names. Every one this forest's lost, in the weft, too fine for him to see. Wherever the tags go, our names go with them.
1. Kill 4 of the wild spiders round the old reeling-house
2. Bring Morwen Teale 3 silk for the names
Bring Morwen Teale 3 silk for the names
Morwen Teale: Forty-four names. Three of them are mine. My husband and both the boys, in the order I'd call them in for supper.
Morwen Teale: Every tag that goes down onto that isle will hang on a cord that knows who it's for. It's not much. It's a thread.
You: You could just not send it.
Morwen Teale: Then he'd have it from the next forest, plain, and nothing would go with them. No. This way something of ours goes where they went.
Morwen Teale: The agent took it. Ran it through his fingers and said it was the best we'd ever made. It is.
Morwen Teale: Forty-four. I hum them while I work. It keeps the count.
: Names woven into the cords. If I'd known how, I'd have put Edrin's into every one.
The Old Man is a side quest, asked by Garrow Penhale (tree-feller, retired). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Garrow Penhale: Thirty years back, the crown wanted the biggest tree in the valley. We called him the Old Man. Took eleven of us nine days to drop him.
Garrow Penhale: They paid in coin, real coin, and hauled him off on forty oxen down the royal road. For the city's moorings, they said. Holding the city to the sky. I told my grandchildren that.
Garrow Penhale: I can't read. There's a plate they nailed on the fellers' post after. Nobody's read it to me in thirty years because I never asked. I'm asking. You've been places.
You: I'll read it for you.
Garrow Penhale: Upslope. The stump you could hold a dance on. The post's on the downhill side.
1. Read the plate on the fellers' post by the Old Man's stump
2. Tell Nessa Vale where the Old Man went
3. Tell Garrow Penhale what the plate says
Read the plate on the fellers' post by the Old Man's stump
"Beside a stump wide enough to hold a dance on, the fellers' post: eleven marks cut by men who couldn't write their names - a fish, an axe, a crooked line, a bird."
"Nailed above them, a brass plate gone green: TIMBER OF THE CROWN. ONE BEAM, FOR THE GREAT CAPSTAN OF THE WORKS BELOW THE STRAIT. YEAR 232. BY ORDER OF THE PRESERVER."
You: Below the strait. Not the city. The capstans down there, where they chain people to the bars.
Tell Nessa Vale where the Old Man went
You: A tree-feller in the redwoods. Thirty years ago his crew dropped a tree for the crown. The plate says it went for a capstan beam, below the strait.
They: Edrin's capstan. The one he pushed. You saw it. Was it wood? Big wood?
You: It was dark. It was big enough to be.
They: Tell the old man it held. Tell him it was good wood and it held my brother up for a year, and turned whatever it turned.
They: Tell him I'd rather it had broken. No. Don't tell him that. Tell him it held.
Tell Garrow Penhale what the plate says
Garrow Penhale: Well? What does it say?
You: It didn't go to the city. It went for a capstan beam, under the sea past Saint Orra's, where the census sent the people it took.
You: A woman whose brother pushed that capstan says to tell you it held.
Garrow Penhale: I told my grandchildren it held up the city. Eleven of us. Nine days. And it went to turn their wheel in the dark.
Garrow Penhale: Take my axe. I've no more use for felling. I'll plant, now, as long as I've got. Something nobody can send for.
Garrow Penhale: Two hundred seedlings in. They'll be giants when nobody remembers either of us.
Garrow Penhale: It held. I keep saying it. It doesn't get easier, but it's true.
: That beam was a tree out of the redwoods. I think about that. Something that had been alive, down there with him.

i: Clemency Ash, who taught school in the city
s: Not a Ruin is a side quest, asked by Clemency Ash (who taught school in the city). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Clemency Ash: I taught the little ones in the service quarter. Letters, sums, the map of the kingdom. I came down on the launch with a satchel of slates and nothing else.
Clemency Ash: The map on my schoolroom wall had the whole country on it. Rivers, the royal road. And nearly every village marked with a little cross. RUIN. Plague, or the wilds, or the old wars.
Clemency Ash: That wall came down out there in the grass when the quarter broke. I can see the plaster from the hedge. I want to know what it says about here.
Clemency Ash: Nineteen years I taught children that nobody lives down here. And a woman's just given me an egg.
Clemency Ash: Past the hedge, where the grass is burned flat. White plaster, blue paint. Mind the edges.
1. Find the fallen schoolroom wall in the grass
2. Ask in the village what Meadham makes of being a ruin
3. Tell Clemency Ash what the map says
Find the fallen schoolroom wall in the grass
"A slab of white plaster wall, gold trim along the top, lying face up in flattened grass. On it, a map of the kingdom in blue and brown, and a child's handprint in one corner."
"Rivers. The royal road. Briar's Rest, with a small cross: RUIN - YEAR 40. Fenn Ford: RUIN - PLAGUE. Village after village, crossed out."
"Here, by the river, a cross and a name: MEADHAM. RUIN - THE WILDS, YEAR 3."
You: Briar's Rest, a ruin. Mara will have something to say about that.
Ask in the village what Meadham makes of being a ruin
They: You're the one walking about with the teacher? Tell her to come in. She stands at my hedge like a cat.
You: Her map says this village has been a ruin since Year 3.
They: Does it. Well, I'm not dead and the hens aren't, and that's my grandfather's barn.
They: We sent grain up every year of my life with MEADHAM on the sack. Somebody up there baked it and ate it and was told we weren't here. That's a strange thing to do to a person.
They: Tell her there's a stool by the fire. And she can teach my grandsons their letters, since the crown never would.
Tell Clemency Ash what the map says
Clemency Ash: Well? What does it say about here?
You: A ruin since Year 3. And Briar's Rest, and Fenn Ford. All of them.
You: Nan Meadham says there's a stool by the fire. And her grandsons want their letters.
Clemency Ash: Since Year 3. I made them copy it out. Neatly. Every cross.
Clemency Ash: ...Letters. I can do letters.
Clemency Ash: Here. It was the quarter's school prize. Nobody's going to win it now, so you have it.
Clemency Ash: Eleven pupils. Muddy. Wonderful. Not one of them believes the city was ever real.
Clemency Ash: I'm painting a new map on Nan's barn. No crosses.
: Briar's Rest, a ruin since Year 40? Tell that teacher to come and say it to my face. Then I'll feed her.
: The city children thought we weren't here? We were here the whole time. We were looking up at them.
The Storm Log is a side quest, asked by Wynn Halloway (storm-watcher). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Wynn Halloway: This post was the crown's once. Storm-watch. A woman sat up here with a glass and a log, and sent word down when weather was coming for the harvest.
Wynn Halloway: They stopped paying sixty years ago. Nobody told the weather, so I kept on.
Wynn Halloway: My log follows my aunt's, and hers follows the woman's before. The oldest books are up at the high post, under the cairn. It's too steep for my knees now.
Wynn Halloway: I want them down before the damp has them. And there's something in them I want to check. It's been keeping me up.
You: I'll fetch the old logs.
Wynn Halloway: Up the spine, past the second false summit. The cairn with an iron lid in it. Mind what lives up there - they like a storm.
1. Clear the things prowling the spine path
2. Find the old storm logs under the cairn at the high post
3. Bring the old storm logs down to Wynn Halloway
Find the old storm logs under the cairn at the high post
"Under the cairn, an iron box, and in it four logbooks wrapped in oilcloth. The oldest is dated in a year with no number - only 'the year of the rising'."
"Day after day, in different hands: wind, cloud, the colour of the sky. And over and over, the same line. 'Bolt at the city. Went round.'"
"'Came straight at the city and turned off it like rain off a sheet. Struck the north peak instead. Lost two goats.'"
"In a later hand: 'Sixty years of this. Never once has it hit. Never once has the cloud round the city moved with the wind.'"
You: Lightning won't touch it. Something over the city turns it aside - and down onto here.
Bring the old storm logs down to Wynn Halloway
Wynn Halloway: Oh, you've got them. Look at that oilcloth. That's my aunt's stitching.
You: They all say the same thing. Lightning goes round the city.
Wynn Halloway: Yes. That's what's been keeping me up. I thought my eyes were going.
Wynn Halloway: Every storm, the bolt bends. And it comes down here instead. On the peaks, on the goats, on this post. I've had the roof off twice.
Wynn Halloway: Whatever keeps the city's sky clean, it's been sweeping the muck off onto ours. Two hundred and sixty years of it, and every one of us wrote it down and nobody read it.
Wynn Halloway: I've started writing it plainer. 'Went round. Hit us.' Somebody should read it one day.
Wynn Halloway: Come up when there's weather. It's the best show there is, as long as you don't mind where it lands.
: Is it true lightning won't hit the city? I'd want it to. Just a little bit. Just on the king.
What the Glass Saw is a side quest, asked by Wynn Halloway (storm-watcher). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Wynn Halloway: You again. Good. I need somebody with legs.

Wynn Halloway: Three nights ago I had the glass on the low country, the way I do, and I saw a light go up from the old landing tower on the plain. Slow. A kite, I'd say - a big one, with a lamp hung under it.
Wynn Halloway: It got as high as the waterfalls. Then the sky went white all round it. Quiet, like sheet lightning with no storm. And the lamp came down.
Wynn Halloway: It came down this side. Behind the third ridge - I marked it. I log weather. I don't know what to log for that.
You: I'll go and find it.
Wynn Halloway: Third ridge, where the scree fans out. I'll keep the glass on you.
1. Find where the flier came down behind the third ridge
2. Take Rob's letter to his mother at the shieling under the ridge
3. Tell Wynn Halloway who the flier was
Find where the flier came down behind the third ridge
"A frame of ash poles and waxed sailcloth, smashed across the scree. In the middle of it, what's left of a young man, burned down one side as though he'd been held to a forge."

"In his coat, a letter folded small. 'Ma - the old men say the tower was for flying up to the city, in the old days, and anyone who got there on their own wing was let in. I'm going to fetch Dacey back. Don't wait up. Rob.'"
You: Nobody told him the old days were over.
Take Rob's letter to his mother at the shieling under the ridge
They: You've come down off the ridge. You've got his coat.
You: I'm sorry. He got as high as the waterfalls.
They: Higher than anyone from this valley's ever been. He'd want that said.
They: He built it all winter in the byre. I sewed the cloth. I thought if I sewed it well enough...
They: Something up there burns people who aren't asked. That's what you're telling me. They take Dacey up for nothing, and they burn the one who goes to fetch her.
They: Then I'll not sew another. Tell the woman with the glass I'm glad she was watching. Somebody should have seen him go.
Tell Wynn Halloway who the flier was
Wynn Halloway: I saw you go down to the shieling. I didn't look after that. I put the glass away.
You: His name was Rob Ashby. The collectors took his sister. He went up to fetch her.
Wynn Halloway: I've written him in the log. Not under weather. I've started a new column.
Wynn Halloway: Here. You'll want something warm under you on the high paths, the way you're going.
Wynn Halloway: The new column's called 'Went up'. There's one name in it. I hope it stays at one.
Wynn Halloway: I don't watch the landing tower any more. I watch the road to it, and if I see a lad with poles on his back, I'm going down there myself.
: A boy built a kite to go and get his sister back? ...Don't tell Tomas. He'd be in the woodshed by tonight with a saw.
Clear All Day is a side quest, asked by Wynn Halloway (storm-watcher). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Wynn Halloway: Look at it. Nothing. Clear from the peaks to the sea. I've never once written 'clear all day'.
Wynn Halloway: I had the glass on it when it went. Watched the whole thing tip into the Crown. Most of an hour. I wrote it down minute by minute, and my hand was going so you can hardly read it.
Wynn Halloway: You told me once there's a little one at your place who asks whether the waterfalls reach the ground. I've watched those falls for forty years. I know the answer.
Wynn Halloway: I've drawn it for her. Will you take it?
You: I'll take it to Pip.
Wynn Halloway: Pip. Good name for a watcher. Carry it flat - don't fold it, I've done the shading.
1. Give Pip the storm-watcher's drawing of the waterfalls
2. Tell Wynn Halloway what Pip said
Give Pip the storm-watcher's drawing of the waterfalls
You: A storm-watcher on the peaks sent you this. She's watched the city's waterfalls for forty years.
They: Is it the answer? Is it about whether they reach?
You: She's drawn it. The water falls a long way, then it goes thin, then it's mist, and the wind takes the mist. It never reached the ground. Not once.
You: Into the clouds. Then it rained. On here, mostly.
They: So it did reach the ground. It just went the long way.
They: Tell her I'm keeping it. Tell her I'll keep it flat.
Tell Wynn Halloway what Pip said
Wynn Halloway: Well? Did she like it?
You: She says it did reach the ground. It just went the long way, as rain.
Wynn Halloway: Forty years with a glass, and a child gets it right in one go. I'll put that in the log.
Wynn Halloway: Weather: clear all day. Observation: Pip was right.
Wynn Halloway: Clear all day again. I'm getting used to writing it.
Wynn Halloway: I gave the old logs to the chapel down the valley. Two hundred and sixty years of 'went round'. Nothing goes round any more. It all just comes down honest.
: The waterfalls went the long way. I've got the drawing. I'm not allowed to fold it, so it lives under my bed, flat.
What the Sink Gave Back is a side quest, asked by Ulla Rensk (herder). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Ulla Rensk: The ground's going soft. It never used to. Every summer the ice underneath melts a bit further down, and the land slumps into ponds.
Ulla Rensk: Last month the pond by the burial knoll took half the knoll with it. My father went in there eight winters back. We hacked at the frost two days to get him down.
Ulla Rensk: Now he's out again, somewhere at the water's edge. I can't go and look. I've done my looking.
Ulla Rensk: Would you find him, and bring stones? We'll lay him on top this time, the old way, where the ground can't change its mind.
Ulla Rensk: Past the three ponds, the one with the dead larch leaning in. He's got a pipe in his hand. We put it in. He'd have come back for it otherwise.
1. Find Ulla's father where the pond took the burial knoll
2. Bring Ulla Rensk 6 stones for a cairn
Find Ulla's father where the pond took the burial knoll
"Bones in the black mud at the water's edge, half out of a slumped bank. A clay pipe still in the hand, the bowl stopped with peat."
"Beside him, deeper in, a second set of bones - older, browner, wrapped in what was a red wool blanket once. A bone comb still in the hair."
You: Two of them. The pond's given back more than she asked for.
Bring Ulla Rensk 6 stones for a cairn
Ulla Rensk: Two? ...A red blanket. A comb.
Ulla Rensk: That's my grandmother. Da always said the frost heaved her marker away and nobody could find her after. He went out looking every spring for thirty years.
Ulla Rensk: And she was there the whole time, a spade's depth under him. The daft old man was lying on top of his own mother.
Ulla Rensk: Stones, good. We'll make it a big one, with the two of them on top where anybody can find them. Here - have one of his pipes. Not that one. He'd haunt me.
Ulla Rensk: The cairn's the tallest thing for a mile. The geese steer by it, I think. Da would like being useful.
Ulla Rensk: The ground keeps going soft. I've started telling people where I want putting. On top. Somewhere high.
The One Under the Ice is a side quest, asked by Hanne Skarr (ice-fisher). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Hanne Skarr: You don't fish the ice here without giving the first one to the One Under. You cut the hole, the first fish goes back down, then you take what you like.
Hanne Skarr: Forty winters I've done it. And for a fortnight something's been at my holes in the night. Lines pulled, the catch gone off the ice, the shelter torn open.
Hanne Skarr: My nephew says it's the One Under, sulking because I've been giving him small fish. I have been giving him small fish. But I'd like to know.
Hanne Skarr: My shelter's out past the reed line. Whatever it is, it's come every night since the new moon.
2. Kill the thing that's been robbing Hanne's ice-holes
3. Tell Hanne Skarr what was taking her fish
"The shelter's hide walls are slashed open. Lines snapped, the drying rack flat. Fish skins everywhere, licked clean."
"Prints in the frost round the hole: big, clawed, and heading for the shore. Not one of them goes near the water."
You: Whatever this is, it didn't come up through the ice. It walked.
Tell Hanne Skarr what was taking her fish
Hanne Skarr: Well? Was it him?
You: It was a beast off the shore. It walked out to your shelter every night and helped itself.
Hanne Skarr: ...Well, that's a relief. And a bit of a let-down, if I'm honest. Forty winters I've been feeding him, and he's never once come up to complain.
Hanne Skarr: I'll keep giving him the first fish. Small ones. He doesn't seem to mind.
Hanne Skarr: Full lines every morning. I gave the One Under a big one, just in case he was watching.
Hanne Skarr: My nephew's sulking. He wanted it to be the One Under. Boys.
The Goat Path is a side quest, asked by Fergal Mott (goatherd). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Fergal Mott: The census cage can't climb. Never could. So up here they do it different - the bell rings down in the valley, and we're meant to walk down to it ourselves.
Fergal Mott: My girl Senna's on the list. Seventeen. I sent her up to the summer shieling with the goats and told the officer she'd gone over the pass to her aunt's.
Fergal Mott: He didn't believe me. There's a patrol coming up the goat path - four of them, and a serjeant who's done this before. They'll be at the shieling by dark.
Fergal Mott: I'm sixty. I've got a crook. I'm asking.
Fergal Mott: The goat path goes up past the waterfall. They'll be slow in all that iron. You won't be.
1. Stop the census patrol on the goat path
2. Tell Senna at the summer shieling the patrol isn't coming
Tell Senna at the summer shieling the patrol isn't coming
They: Who are you? Did Da send you? Is it the patrol?
You: It was. They won't be coming up the path.
They: They'll send others. They always send others. Our Kit walked down to the bell three summers ago and got into the cage like a good lad, because he was told to.
They: ...I'm not walking down. I'll go over the pass to my aunt's for real now. Da can tell them the truth this time.
They: Tell him to keep the brown nanny. She's the only one who listens to him.
Fergal Mott: She went over at first light. I watched her to the top. She didn't look back, which is how I taught her.
Fergal Mott: The brown nanny's mine now. Senna was right. She listens.
: A girl on the list just walked off over the mountains? You can do that? ...I'm only asking.
The Pay-Shed Tally is a side quest, asked by Dunstan Coe (royal miner, retired). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Dunstan Coe: You went down the Last Vein. Word gets round the pits. Did you hear it? The bell?
Dunstan Coe: I cut stone in the royal mines forty years. The Last Vein was the deepest, and the crown paid best for the lower gallery. Double, for a shift down there.
Dunstan Coe: Men went down for double, and some didn't come up. For every one, the crown sent the widow a purse and a paper saying rockfall.
Dunstan Coe: I kept no list. I wish I had. But the pay-shed by the old adit kept one. There's a tally box under the floor. I want to see it before I die - and I'm working on that.
Dunstan Coe: The pay-shed by the old adit, up the switchback. The floor's rotten. The box is under where the clerk's stool was.
1. Find the tally box under the old pay-shed
2. Read Dunstan Coe the pay-shed tally
3. Show Oren Flint the pay-shed tally
Find the tally box under the old pay-shed
"A tin-lined box under rotten boards. Inside, a ledger in a clerk's tidy hand: shifts, names, pay. Double for the lower gallery."
"Beside some names, a small mark inked in red - the royal census mark. Every man with the mark was 'lost to rockfall' within the month."
"At the back, one page in the same hand, pressed so hard it's torn: 'The lower gallery has no rock to fall. It has a door. They hand them through it. I have seen it. W. Pask, clerk.'"
You: They weren't lost. They were sent down - and paid double for the walk.
Read Dunstan Coe the pay-shed tally
Dunstan Coe: Read it to me. My eyes are gone for small writing.
You: Every man marked in red was lost to 'rockfall'. The clerk wrote that the lower gallery has a door, and they handed men through it.
Dunstan Coe: Pask. Walter Pask. He hanged himself in that shed. We said it was the drink.
Dunstan Coe: My brother Aldo's in there, isn't he. In red.
Dunstan Coe: Take it to somebody who mends things. I hear there's a smith down your way whose tools came up out of that mine. He should know what he was standing over.
Show Oren Flint the pay-shed tally
You: A ledger from the royal mines' pay-shed. The men marked in red never came up. The clerk says they were handed through a door in the lower gallery.
They: The lower gallery. I've seen that stone. Dressed too well for miners, and a barred hole going down, and that bell under it.
They: The crown paid me silver for wagon-work, back when. I thought I was being paid for being good with iron.
They: Leave it with me. I'll make it a box that'll outlast the both of us.
Dunstan Coe: Aldo. I've said his name more this week than in thirty years. It helps, oddly.
Dunstan Coe: They tell me the bell in the Vein still rings. Somebody should shut that door. I'm too old. You're not.
: That ledger's in an iron box by my anvil. Every time I strike, I think of a clerk named Pask.

i: Hob Nettleby, keeper of the storm chapel
s: Struck is a side quest, asked by Hob Nettleby (keeper of the storm chapel). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Hob Nettleby: Up here we marry in thunderstorms. Under the chapel rod. You wait for a good one, you hold hands, and the rod takes the bolt while you say the words.
Hob Nettleby: If it strikes during the vows, it's a struck marriage, and those last. My parents were struck. Fifty-one years, and they never once agreed about anything.
Hob Nettleby: Somebody's had the rod. Copper fetches a lot from the wrong people, and the wrong people have been about. And I've a couple who've been waiting since spring for a decent storm.
Hob Nettleby: They won't marry under a chapel that might take the bolt itself. Nor would I.
You: I'll see about the copper.
Hob Nettleby: The thieves'll be camped somewhere along the scarp. Get me the copper back - or any copper - and I'll have a rod up before the next front.
1. Deal with the copper thieves along the scarp
2. Bring Hob Nettleby 2 copper ingots for a new chapel rod
Bring Hob Nettleby 2 copper ingots for a new chapel rod
Hob Nettleby: Copper! Not my copper - mine had a green on it you could tell the season by. But copper.
Hob Nettleby: Ninety years that rod was up. Every bolt that hit this plateau in my lifetime came down it, near enough.
Hob Nettleby: I'll have it drawn and up by tonight. There's a front coming from the south, and Ebba and Jory have been sat in their good clothes since breakfast.
Hob Nettleby: Stay for it, if you like. Stand well back. The struck ones always say it was the loudest thing they ever heard, and the best.
Hob Nettleby: Struck on the second vow. Ebba's hair stood up for an hour. They'll last.
Hob Nettleby: Folk ask me why the bolts never hit the city. I tell them the city's never married anybody.
The Count is a side quest, asked by Maren Holt (trapper). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Maren Holt: Keep your voice down. I've a man in my woodshed who used to wear blue.

Maren Holt: He walked off from Three Toll in the autumn with half the garrison. The others went home. He came north, as far from the road as he could get. Now there's a party from the fort combing the taiga for him.
Maren Holt: He's no use to me. Eats like two. But he cried the first night, and soldiers don't cry about nothing.
Maren Holt: Thin out the ones looking, and he'll go up to my old trapline cabin where they'll never think to look. Then go and see him. He's got something to give someone who's walking the road.
You: I'll deal with the search party.
Maren Holt: They go in pairs along the river, mostly. Don't let them see which way you came.
1. Thin out the crown soldiers searching the taiga
2. Find the deserter at Maren's old trapline cabin
Find the deserter at Maren's old trapline cabin
They: Maren sent you? Then I'll say it quick, before I lose my nerve again.
They: At Three Toll we counted cages. Not people - cages. A cage comes through with forty tags on it, it leaves with forty tags. That's the count. It's all anybody up the road ever checks.
They: If one dies, or runs, the escort fills the tag. Whoever's nearest the road. A drover. A girl with eggs. Doesn't matter. The tag's stitched already.
They: I filled two myself. A tinker and his boy. I never asked their names. They had names on them already - somebody else's.
They: Because you're walking the road, and someone ought to know it's the count they care about. Not who. Here - my tag-awl. I don't want it in my hand again.
Maren Holt: He's at the cabin. He sets every snare twice and sends me down the hares. It's a sort of apology. Not to me.
Maren Holt: If anyone in blue asks, I've never had a man in my woodshed in my life. Which is true now.
: Whoever's nearest the road. Edrin was on the road to market that morning. I always wondered why it was him.

i: Arvo Lind, back from Saint Orra's
s: Nobody at Sallow Tarn is a side quest, asked by Arvo Lind (back from Saint Orra's). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Arvo Lind: You opened my cell. You won't remember. There were a lot of us, and we all looked the same by then.
Arvo Lind: I walked north a month to get home. Sallow Tarn. Twelve houses, a smoke-shed, the best smoked char on the barrens. And there's nobody. Doors open, hearths cold, the goats gone wild.
Arvo Lind: They took me eight years ago. I thought it was just me. I've not dared walk round the far side of the tarn, where the bell frame stood. Would you?
Arvo Lind: Round the far side, past the smoke-shed. If there's a post there, I know what'll be on it. I want to be wrong.
1. Find what stands where the bell frame was at Sallow Tarn
2. Follow the boot-prints north into the barrens
3. Find whoever keeps the camp on the barrens
Find what stands where the bell frame was at Sallow Tarn
"A post where a bell frame stood, nailed thick with census tags, faded and curled. Thirty of them. More."
"Every name in the village, by the look of it, each with RECEIVED stitched first. Three Linds. ARVO LIND is here too - dated a year after the boat took him."
"One nail is bare but for a scrap of linen, torn off, not cut. Small boot-prints in the old mud lead away north into the barrens, and back, and away again. Recent."
You: They took the whole village, and counted him twice. But somebody's been coming back here.
Follow the boot-prints north into the barrens
"A camp in the lee of a boulder: a turf wall, a fire still warm under the ash, a line of fish skins drying."
"A linen tag is pinned to the turf like a holy picture. ODA LIND. SALLOW TARN. RECEIVED. The word RECEIVED has been unpicked, stitch by stitch, with a needle. Only the holes are left."
You: She took her own tag off their post. And took their word out of it.
Find whoever keeps the camp on the barrens
They: Stop there. I've a spear, and I'm better with it than I look.
You: Arvo Lind's come home. He's back from the isle. He's at the tarn.
They: I hid in the smoke-shed when the bell went. Under the char racks. Eight years I've been out here watching the road to see who'd come back up it. Nobody does.
They: I took my name off their post. Unpicked their word. I wasn't received. I'm here.
They: Tell him his aunt's coming home. Tell him to clean the smoke-shed. I'm not sleeping in it again.
Arvo Lind: She's cleaning the smoke-shed herself. She says I do it wrong. I've never been so glad to be told I do something wrong.
Arvo Lind: Two of us at Sallow Tarn. It's a village, if you squint.
: Eight years alone on the barrens, and she unpicked the word out of her own tag. I'd like to meet that woman.

i: Sister Hild, keeper of the Penitents
s: The Penitents is a side quest, asked by Sister Hild (keeper of the Penitents). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Sister Hild: You know why they call them the Penitents? The spikes. They all lean the same way, like people kneeling into the wind.
Sister Hild: When someone from the valleys is collected, their family climbs up here, and I cut the name into one. It's a hard way up. They come anyway. I've cut three hundred and eleven.

Sister Hild: They say people are walking up out of the ground now. Up a stair under the sea, out of pens. There's one living under the ridge who came up that way. He won't come near the Penitents. He says they look like a queue.
Sister Hild: Would you take him my list? If he knows any of them... I'd like to know which ones to keep.
You: I'll take him the list.
Sister Hild: Under the overhang at the ridge foot. Aske Morrow. Be gentle. And don't ring anything near him - he goes white at bells.
1. Take Sister Hild's list to Aske Morrow under the ridge
2. Tell Sister Hild what Aske Morrow knew
Take Sister Hild's list to Aske Morrow under the ridge
They: A list. Course it's a list.
You: Sister Hild's. The names she's cut in the ice. She wants to know if you saw any of them below.
They: ...Gil Harrow. Big laugh, too big for down there. He was on the capstans next to me. Alive when I came up, if you call it that.
They: Bet Corran. She was in the line for the Furnace. I watched her go through the door. I'm sorry.
They: The rest, I don't know. There were thousands. You don't learn names down there. They give you a number, and you learn that.
They: Tell her not to cut any more. Tell her it's not like kneeling. It's like standing in a line for a door.
Tell Sister Hild what Aske Morrow knew
Sister Hild: You saw him? Did he...?
You: Gil Harrow's alive, on the capstans. Bet Corran went into the Furnace. The rest he doesn't know. He says don't cut any more.
Sister Hild: I thought I'd melt Bet's. A torch and a prayer, and let her go into the ground as water. I don't think I can make myself.
Sister Hild: I'll leave them all standing. The ice doesn't know who's dead either, and it hasn't stopped kneeling.
Sister Hild: But I won't cut any more. He's right. Not because there won't be names. Because I'd rather somebody went down and fetched them.
Sister Hild: Gil Harrow's mother came up yesterday and sat by his spike all day. I didn't tell her to stop hoping. I hadn't the right.
Sister Hild: Aske came up as far as the first row. Stood there a long while. Then he turned his back on them and said that felt better.
: Three hundred and eleven names cut in ice. Edrin would've been one of them, if I'd made the climb. He's in this house instead. I keep checking.
When the Bell Stopped is a side quest, asked by Mag Penhallow (column-cutter). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Mag Penhallow: We cut columns here. The basalt comes up out of the ground in six-sided posts, ready made. You snap them off the top and sell them for gateposts.

Mag Penhallow: At the end of the causeway there's a shaft where the columns go down further than any line we've got. A bell's hung over it since before my great-grandad. It rings from below. Always has. We set our shifts by it.
Mag Penhallow: Three days ago it stopped. In the middle of a stroke. Then things started climbing out.
Mag Penhallow: Dead things. Old, in old chains. They come up out of the shaft and stand about in the rain like they've forgotten what for, and then they go for whoever's nearest.
Mag Penhallow: They're all along the causeway. Then look at the bell for me. I want to know it's really done, and not just catching its breath.
1. Put down the dead climbing out of the causeway shaft
2. Look at the bell over the shaft at the causeway's end
3. Tell Mag Penhallow about the bell
Look at the bell over the shaft at the causeway's end
"A heavy bell on a frame of black timber at the shaft's lip. The shaft breathes up warm air that smells of a forge gone out."

"The royal census mark is cut into the bronze, and under it the sign from the gateway below. Both are split clean through - one long crack from crown to lip, as though the bell were struck once, too hard, from inside."
You: It was struck the moment whatever held it stopped holding. It won't ring again.
Tell Mag Penhallow about the bell
Mag Penhallow: Well? Is it done?
You: It's cracked through, mark and all. Whatever rang it isn't there any more.
Mag Penhallow: Two hundred years we set our shifts by that bell. My grandad called it the hill's heart.
Mag Penhallow: It's not, is it. You know what it was. I can see it on you.
You: It was a doorbell. For something nobody should ever have answered.
Mag Penhallow: ...Right. Then we'll haul it up and melt it, and cast one for the chapel that rings when we ring it. I'll make it a good one. Here - for the walking you do.
Mag Penhallow: We hauled it up. Twelve of us on the rope. The shaft's just a shaft now - cold air and a long drop.
Mag Penhallow: The new bell's got a crack-line cast into it on purpose. So we remember.
: A bell on the Causeway that cracked itself the moment it was finished? I wish the one in the Vein had the same manners.

i: Ottilie Marr, of the grooms' line
s: The Grooms' Rule is a side quest, asked by Ottilie Marr (of the grooms' line). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Ottilie Marr: You're the one with the wyvern. Everybody in the Needles knows. The goats haven't stopped screaming.
Ottilie Marr: My people were grooms. Before the city went up, the riders lived on the needles and we kept their beasts - fed them, mended harness, sang them down in bad weather.

Ottilie Marr: When the city rose, crown men came and broke the perches and burned the saddles. Flying was the king's now. The beasts went wild. We stayed, and kept the song that calls them down, and nobody's needed it in two hundred and sixty years.
Ottilie Marr: Up there it's cold like nothing you know. The riders froze, mostly. They didn't fall - they froze, and then they fell. Let me make you what they wore. I'll need things.
Ottilie Marr: An old nest first. On the high needle, the one with the split top. The riders left something in every nest. If it's still there, I'll know where to start.
1. Search the old wyvern nest on the split-topped needle
2. Bring Ottilie Marr 6 feathers for a rider's hood
Search the old wyvern nest on the split-topped needle
"A great nest of split branches and bone, wedged in the needle's cleft. Old - grey and brittle - and empty but for shell as thick as pottery."
"Wired to the biggest branch: a bronze ring, rider's work, engraved inside. 'KEEP HER WARM AND SHE KEEPS YOU UP. The Grooms' Rule.'"
Bring Ottilie Marr 6 feathers for a rider's hood
Ottilie Marr: The Rule. My grandmother taught me that before she taught me my name.
Ottilie Marr: Feathers, good. Leather outside, felt in the middle, down against the skin. That's how they went up.
Ottilie Marr: The beast keeps itself warm. You don't. Your hands go first, then your sense. A rider who stops shivering is a rider about to let go.
Ottilie Marr: Here. Put it on and sing this with me, once. It isn't for her. It's for you - to keep your mouth moving, so you know you're still awake.
Ottilie Marr: The first flier off our needles since the city rose. My grandmother would have been unbearable about it.
Ottilie Marr: Stop shivering, you let go. Remember that, up there.
: Felt and feathers, and a song to keep you awake? Good. I've seen what cold does to fingers. Wear it.
The True Bushel is a side quest, asked by Dorrit Kell (salt-panner). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Dorrit Kell: Forty pounds to the tithe bushel. That's what the weigh-stone at the old salt road says, and that's what the collectors take, every autumn, off every pan on the flat.
Dorrit Kell: My gran raked salt here sixty years. She always said a crown bushel was thirty. Said it like she'd been robbed, and we laughed at her, because she said that about everything.

Dorrit Kell: There's a milestone out on the royal road, past the last pans, where the weighhouse stood. They cut the measures into the milestones in the first years, so nobody could argue. Go and see what it says. If Gran was right, I owe her an apology, and she's been dead nine years.
Dorrit Kell: Follow the road posts west. Don't walk on the crust where it's grey - it's thin, and the brine under it is deep.
1. Read the king's measures on the old milestone past the salt pans
2. Tell Dorrit Kell what the milestone says
Read the king's measures on the old milestone past the salt pans
"A milestone of pale stone, half sunk in salt, the gold of the royal mark worn down to a few flecks in the grooves."
"Cut deep along one face, in an old square hand: THE KING'S MEASURES. A BUSHEL OF SALT: XXX POUNDS. A BUSHEL OF GRAIN: L POUNDS. YEAR 3."
"The XXX has a fourth X cut after it, newer and shallower, the edges still sharp. Someone has done the same to the grain: the L is now LX."
You: Nobody changed the law. Somebody came out here with a chisel.
Tell Dorrit Kell what the milestone says
Dorrit Kell: Well? Was she mad, or was I?
You: Thirty, cut in the first years. Somebody's added a ten since, with a chisel. The grain's had the same done to it.
Dorrit Kell: A chisel. Not even a proclamation. A man with a chisel on a quiet afternoon.
Dorrit Kell: Ten pounds a pan, every autumn, for... no, I'll not work it out. I'd only have to sit down.
Dorrit Kell: Here. Salt's the one thing I've too much of. Gran would want you to have the good stuff, from the bottom of the pan.
Dorrit Kell: I went out and sat by the milestone and said sorry to her. Out loud. The other panners think I've gone soft.
Dorrit Kell: If the collectors come this autumn, I'll give them thirty and tell them to bring their chisel.
: Somebody chiselled the salt measure up by a third? I've loaded crown carts heavier than the book said. I always thought it was me, counting wrong.
What the Dune Gave Back is a side quest, asked by Ammon Reyle (caravan guide). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Ammon Reyle: Twenty-two years I've walked caravans across this sand. One I lost.
Ammon Reyle: A census convoy. Six soldiers and a cage, going east to the royal road. They paid me in crown silver to take them the short way, between the big dunes. The wind came up the second day.
Ammon Reyle: I walked out. Walking out's my trade. They didn't, and nor did the six in the cage. Never a sign of any of it.

Ammon Reyle: Last month the big dune moved off. They do, every twenty years or so, like a cow getting up. The drovers say there's iron sticking out of the sand where it was. I can't go. I've tried. My legs won't.
Ammon Reyle: Between the two tallest dunes, where the sand's gone hard and dark. Go early. You don't want to be out there when it comes up hot.
1. Find the census cage the dune uncovered
2. Search for the convoy's soldiers near the cage
3. Tell Ammon Reyle what the dune gave back
Find the census cage the dune uncovered
"A census cage, scoured bright by the sand on one side and rusted black on the other. The blue board has lost its paint; the gold mark is a smooth dent."
"The door is shut and locked. Two bars beside it have been cut through - not broken, cut, slowly, the ends filed smooth."
"Six linen tags hung on the bars once. Five strings are bare, the knots picked loose by hand. One tag is left: HOB ASHER. TALLOW. 9-31. RECEIVED."
You: Somebody sat in there with a file and took their time. And took their names with them, all but one.
Search for the convoy's soldiers near the cage
"Bones in a heap of rotted canvas, a soldier's helmet, a crossbow with its string gone. They sheltered here, and the sand came over them."

"A leather book in a tin case. The last page, in a cramped hand: 'Day 2. Storm. Guide gone. Cage 9 fast in the sand, contents quiet. If found, Cage 9 to be entered as delivered. Receipts are signed.'"
You: Contents quiet. They were quiet because they were busy.
Tell Ammon Reyle what the dune gave back
Ammon Reyle: You found it. I can see you did.
You: The cage was locked, but two bars were filed through and five of the tags were taken. The soldiers are under the sand with their book. They wrote the cage up as delivered.
Ammon Reyle: Filed through. With what? They'd been searched. I watched them searched.
Ammon Reyle: ...Five got out. Five, out of the sand, with no guide, and I walked off and never looked back.
You: One tag was left. Hob Asher.
Ammon Reyle: Hob. Big lad, a chandler's boy. Shoulders on him like a door. He'd never have got through a gap two bars wide.
Ammon Reyle: Thank you. I've been carrying six. I can put five of them down.
Ammon Reyle: Five. I say it to myself at night. Five.
Ammon Reyle: There's herders out east on the grass who walked in out of the sand once, people say. I always thought it was a story.
: Somebody filed through a census cage? With a file? I want to know how. I just want to know, that's all.

i: Ammon Reyle, caravan guide, far from the sand
s: Already Received is a side quest, asked by Ammon Reyle (caravan guide, far from the sand). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Ammon Reyle: You'll think I followed you. I didn't. I followed a story.

Ammon Reyle: The herders here talk about a woman who walked in out of the desert, years back, with a file in her boot and three people behind her. They call her the Sand Wife. They say the census can't see her.
Ammon Reyle: She keeps cattle out past the baobabs. I've been three days getting up the nerve. I was the guide. She'll know my face.
You: I'll go and talk to her.
Ammon Reyle: Past the big baobabs, at the cattle pens. Tell her who sent you. Or don't, if you think that's kinder.
1. Find the Sand Wife at the cattle pens past the baobabs
2. Tell Ammon Reyle what the Sand Wife said
3. Tell Nessa Vale about the woman who got out of a census cage
Find the Sand Wife at the cattle pens past the baobabs
They: Ammon Reyle sent you. He's been sat under that tree three days like a dropped sack. The herd boys told me.
You: He wants to know how you got out.
They: A file. My husband baked it into the loaf he gave me at the bell. The soldiers broke the bread open looking for coins and never looked in the crust.
They: Two nights' work. Four of us went through. Hob couldn't. He held the bars steady and sang, so they wouldn't hear the file.

They: Here's the bit nobody believes. Three years back the bell rang here. The officer read the list, and my name was on it. He looked at me, and he looked at his paper, and he said 'Already received.' And went next door.
They: On their paper I've been in the city twenty-two years. It's very restful.
Tell Ammon Reyle what the Sand Wife said
Ammon Reyle: Well? Did she ask about me?
You: She knew you were here. Her husband baked a file into the bread. Four got out. Hob held the bars and sang so the soldiers wouldn't hear the filing.
Ammon Reyle: He sang. I remember now. The first night - I thought it was the wind in the bars.
You: The census came for her again three years ago. The officer read her name, checked his list and said she was already received.
Ammon Reyle: Already received. So that's what the paper's for. Once it says you've gone, you've gone, whoever's standing in front of them.
Ammon Reyle: Take this. It's walked me out of every storm but one. I'll not need it - I'm going to sit under her tree till she'll talk to me. And you know someone who'd want to hear this. I can tell.
Tell Nessa Vale about the woman who got out of a census cage

You: A woman on the grass got out of a census cage twenty-two years ago, with a file baked in bread. The crown's book says she was delivered. When the bell came for her again, the officer read her name and walked past.
They: ...Got out. Out of a cage.
They: Edrin's paper says he volunteered. Hers says she was delivered. The paper doesn't care what happened. It only cares that it's filled in.
They: Which means it can be wrong. I've wanted somebody to show me that for a year.
They: Bread. Her man put it in the bread. I should have thought of that.
Ammon Reyle: She let me sit at the pens yesterday. Didn't speak. Handed me a bowl of milk. I'm counting that.
Ammon Reyle: When soldiers on the road ask my business now, I say 'already received'. They don't know what to do with it.
: A file in a loaf. I think about it every time Mara bakes.
: Is it true a lady ran away from the soldiers with bread? Can I have the bread with the thing in it?
The Waymarks is a side quest, asked by Habb Treese (waymarker). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Habb Treese: See the cairns? Bones, stacked, every few hundred paces out across the white. That's the old road, the safe one. The royal stones were carted off long ago, so we mark it the old way.
Habb Treese: Out here, when you die, you get to be useful. My father's the third cairn from the well. My aunt's the one with the lean. We're a practical people.

Habb Treese: Something's been at them. Pulling them down at night and dragging the long bones off to chew. Two gone this month. A road with gaps in it's worse than no road - people trust it, and then it isn't there.
You: I'll deal with whatever's doing it.
Habb Treese: They come in off the scrub after dark. Kill a few and the rest'll go elsewhere. Then bring me bone, any bone, and I'll build the gaps back.
1. Kill 5 of the creatures pulling down the bone cairns
2. Bring Habb Treese 5 bones to rebuild the cairns
Bring Habb Treese 5 bones to rebuild the cairns
Habb Treese: Good bone, that. Whose was it? No - don't tell me. Out here it doesn't matter whose it was. It matters where it's put.
Habb Treese: There. Gaps filled. Anyone walking in from the well tonight walks home.
You: You don't mind? Strangers' bones in your father's road?
Habb Treese: He'd be glad of the company. He never could stand a gap in a wall.
Habb Treese: You've earned a place, you know. When it's your turn, come out here. We'll find you a good spot. Facing the well.
Habb Treese: A lad walked in from the far wells last night following the cairns. Didn't even know they were people. That's how it should be.
Habb Treese: My aunt's still leaning. She always did.
: Habb Treese's cairns? My sister and I walked that road once, when we were young and stupid. We counted his father.
The Painted City is a side quest, asked by Lell Ashby (ochre-grinder). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Lell Ashby: I grind ochre. Reds, yellows, a brown you'd sell your mother for. Folk came from all over for it, when folk went anywhere.

Lell Ashby: My grandmother's grandmother's grandmother painted the shrine up on the mesa shoulder, and every generation of us touches it up. It's my turn. I've never been up. I can't abide heights, and it's a family secret that I can't.
Lell Ashby: Go and look at it for me? Tell me what's faded worst, so I know what colours to grind.
You: I'll look at the painting.
Lell Ashby: Up the goat path on the shoulder. Don't look down. I never have, which is how I've never been up.
1. Look at the painted shrine on the mesa shoulder
2. Bring Lell Ashby 3 amber to grind for the red figures
Look at the painted shrine on the mesa shoulder
"A little shrine cut back into the red rock, painted floor to roof. The colours are old, and still bright where the sun doesn't reach."

"On the left wall: a city on a hill, white walls and gold roofs, people at its gates with carts and goats. On the right: the same city high on a blue sky, its foundations hanging down like roots - and where the hill was, a black hole, painted thick."
"Between the two, a line of small red figures walks towards the hole. The red has worn worst of all. Someone has touched up each figure, carefully, for a very long time."
You: The city stood on the ground once. And the first thing anyone painted after it rose was people walking into the hole it left.
Bring Lell Ashby 3 amber to grind for the red figures
Lell Ashby: The little red people. It's always the little red people. My mother said the same.
You: They're walking into the hole where the city stood.
Lell Ashby: We always called them the pilgrims. Going to see where the city was, my gran said.
Lell Ashby: ...You don't look like you think they're pilgrims.
Lell Ashby: Well. Dragonblood off the plateau trees. It's the only red that lasts. I'll do them properly this year, every one, and count them as I go.
Lell Ashby: Thirty-one of them. I counted. I'd always thought there were twelve.
Lell Ashby: I went up the goat path and painted them myself. Didn't look down. I'm not telling anyone.
: Was the city really on the ground once? Then were the waterfalls just rivers?
A Tithe of Cattle is a side quest, asked by Rennick Farrow (herdsman). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Rennick Farrow: Men came through last week in crown blue with a census banner. Read out a tithe of cattle - one beast in five - and showed us the seal on the paper. Took twenty-two head.
Rennick Farrow: I paid. You pay. Everyone pays.

Rennick Farrow: Then I got to thinking. Real collectors have come here twice in my life, and both times they took cattle and people. This lot never looked at the people. Didn't even count my boy. I've never known the crown forget a boy.
Rennick Farrow: They're camped past the waterhole, by their smoke. If I'm wrong, I've lost nothing but your afternoon.
Rennick Farrow: Past the waterhole, where the grass is flattened. Twenty-two head. I'd know every one of them.
1. Find the census men's camp past the waterhole
2. Deal with Lark Tolley and his census men
3. Tell Rennick Farrow what his tithe went to
Find the census men's camp past the waterhole
"A camp of trampled grass and cattle dung. Blue tunics hang drying on a thorn bush - dyed, badly. The colour's coming off on the thorns."
"By the fire, a seal: a yam, cut flat, the royal mark carved into it with a knife. Close enough, in poor light, for a herder who's been taught never to look at the mark too long."
"A tally-stick beside it, notched: four herds this month."
You: They've made people so afraid of the seal that a carved yam will do.
Tell Rennick Farrow what his tithe went to
Rennick Farrow: You're back, and not running. So.
You: Thieves in dyed tunics. Their seal was a yam with the mark carved in it. Your cattle are by the waterhole.
Rennick Farrow: I bowed to a yam. I stood in my own yard with my hat off and bowed to a vegetable.
Rennick Farrow: You know what gave them away? They left my boy. That's the joke of it. The real ones would have taken him too.
Rennick Farrow: Take the hides, and the dried meat. We're killing one tonight to celebrate, and there's nobody I'd rather owe.
Rennick Farrow: My boy's taken to bowing to yams. I can't make him stop.
Rennick Farrow: Twenty-one head back. One they ate. I'd have done the same.
: A seal cut in a yam. I've seen real ones up close. Honestly? I'm not sure I'd have known.
Tithe of Heat is a side quest, asked by Garrick Smale (charcoal-burner). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Garrick Smale: I burn charcoal. Wood in a mound, turf over it, nine days of slow fire, and you sit with it every hour of the nine. Leave a clamp alone and it either goes out or goes up.
Garrick Smale: My lad's gone to the coast for salt and I've a clamp to build and not enough cut. My back's done. There's a sack in it for you.
Garrick Smale: Six good lengths. Not the cinder trees - they're half burned already.
1. Bring Garrick Smale 6 wood for his charcoal clamp
2. Look in the crown charcoal cart in the ditch by the old road
3. Tell Garrick Smale what was in the cart
Bring Garrick Smale 6 wood for his charcoal clamp
Garrick Smale: Good. Dry. That'll take.
Garrick Smale: Sit a minute while I turf it. It's dull work. You get to thinking.
Garrick Smale: My grandad sold every sack to the crown. Carts came up the old road twice a year empty and went down loaded. More than all the forges on the coast could ever burn.

Garrick Smale: He wondered where it went his whole life. There's one of those carts still in the ditch by the old road, where it went over. He'd never go near it. Have a look on your way, if you like. I'll be here nine days.
Look in the crown charcoal cart in the ditch by the old road
"A crown cart on its side in the ditch, its wheels gone to the spokes. Charcoal dust has worked into every crack of the wood, black as a chimney."
"A tin box nailed under the seat holds a waybill: CINDERWOOD CHARCOAL - 60 SACKS. TO REEDWAKE, FOR SHIPPING ONWARD. NOT FOR THE FORGES OF THE ROAD. ACCOUNT: TITHE OF HEAT."
"Below it, in another hand: 'Last year 60. This year they ask 90. What are they warming?'"
You: A tithe of heat. Paid in charcoal, and shipped out to sea.
Tell Garrick Smale what was in the cart
Garrick Smale: You've the look of someone who's read something.
You: A waybill. Sixty sacks to Reedwake, shipped on from there. Not for the road forges. The account was called the Tithe of Heat.
Garrick Smale: Shipped. There's nothing out past Reedwake but sea and that island with the monks on it.
Garrick Smale: Monks don't burn ninety sacks a year. Monks are cold. Everyone knows that about monks.
Garrick Smale: Here's your sack, and a bit over. If you're ever down that way and you see a chimney on the water, you come and tell me.
Garrick Smale: Nine days, and the clamp came out lovely. I kept thinking about those ninety sacks.
Garrick Smale: Ninety. What do you warm with ninety sacks?
: Cinderwood charcoal? We were never allowed it. Crown's, they said. I used to watch it go past on the road and burn peat.
The Black Seam is a side quest, asked by Bet Tasker (knapper). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Bet Tasker: You'll not have seen a proper glass blade. Here. Hold it to the light - you can see the mountain through it. The edge'd shave a gnat.
Bet Tasker: Folk say obsidian remembers the fire that made it. Put a flake to your ear on a still night and you'll hear the mountain grumble. That's not superstition. That's knapping.
Bet Tasker: My grandson Tam's run off up to the black seam - the pure glass, up by the vents - with my good hammer, because I told him he wasn't ready. He's not. And it's been two days.
Bet Tasker: Up the slope where the ground goes shiny. He'll have camped somewhere stupid. Bring him back with all his fingers. And the hammer.
1. Find Tam's camp on the glassy slope
2. Kill the beast prowling the slope above Tam's camp
3. Find Tam up on the black seam
4. Bring Tam back down to Bet Tasker
Find Tam's camp on the glassy slope
"A cold fire on the glassy ground, a blanket, a heap of flakes - bad ones, struck too hard, shattered rather than split."
"A note on a flat stone, weighted with a flake: 'Gone up to the seam proper. Don't tell Gran I took the good hammer. If you are Gran, I didn't.'"
"Something big has walked through the camp since. The flakes are crushed into the ground in a line, going uphill."
You: He's further up. So is whatever made those tracks.
Find Tam up on the black seam
They: Is it dead? Properly? I've been up here a day and a half. It kept walking past.
They: Oh no. Did she say about the hammer?
They: Look, though. Pure seam, black right through, not a bubble in it. I've struck six blades off it and they're all better than hers. Don't tell her that.
They: And put your ear to the rock. Go on. Hear it? Grumbling, way down. She says that's the mountain. It doesn't sound like a mountain to me. It sounds like something working.
Bring Tam back down to Bet Tasker
Bet Tasker: There he is. All his fingers? Count them for me, I can't look.
You: All ten, and the hammer. He's struck six blades off the pure seam. He says to tell you they're not as good as yours.
Bet Tasker: He says that, does he. Give me one.
Bet Tasker: ...Oh, the little devil. That's better than mine. That's better than my mother's.
Bet Tasker: Here. One of his - he owes you that. And don't you ever tell him what I said.
Bet Tasker: He's insufferable now. I'm so proud I could spit.
Bet Tasker: He keeps putting his ear to the rock and saying it doesn't sound like a mountain. I've told him to stop. He's frightening the goats.
The Counting Book is a side quest, asked by Ottilie Brack (geyser-counter). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.

Ottilie Brack: Forty-one years I've counted the geysers. Every spout, every hour, in the book. The Old Kettle goes every seventy minutes and has since before my mother. You could set the church by it, if we had one.

Ottilie Brack: This spring a new vent opened past the white terraces. It doesn't keep time like the others. It goes when it pleases. And things crawl up out of it, wet and hot, so I can't get close to see what it throws.
Ottilie Brack: I built a cairn to mark it. Clear the creatures, and look at what's piled round the cairn. I'll want it exactly. Everything goes in the book.
You: I'll go to the new vent.
Ottilie Brack: Past the white terraces. Watch your feet - the crust there's thin as a pie and twice as hot.
1. Kill 4 of the wild things crawling up from the new vent
2. Look at what the new vent has thrown up round Ottilie's cairn
3. Tell Ottilie Brack what the vent throws up
Look at what the new vent has thrown up round Ottilie's cairn
"Ottilie's cairn, stained yellow and white by the spray. Round its foot the vent has laid down a crust of mineral, and in it, scattered like seed, small rings of blackened brass."
"Dozens. Each a little eyelet, the size you'd punch in linen to tie it on with string. A few still hold a scorched thread."
You: Something under here is hot enough to burn linen off brass. And there's a great deal of linen.
Tell Ottilie Brack what the vent throws up
Ottilie Brack: Well? I've the book open.
You: Brass eyelets. Dozens, burned black, thrown up with the water. The kind they put in census tags.
Ottilie Brack: I'll write it down. Everything goes in the book.

Ottilie Brack: Here's something else for it. I went back through the pages last night. The new vent goes hardest on bell days. Every time I've heard of the census bell ringing - Fenn Ford, Three Toll, along the coast - the next spout's the big one.
Ottilie Brack: I'd thought it was the ground. Now I don't know what I think. Take this. It was my mother's, from the first book. I want it somewhere that isn't here.
Ottilie Brack: I've started a new column in the book. I don't know what to head it.
Ottilie Brack: It went big this morning. I don't know where the bell was. Somewhere.
: Brass off census tags, coming up out of the ground hot. Don't tell me any more. I'll ask when I want to know.
Pitch for the Boats is a side quest, asked by Dunstan Pyle (tar-boiler). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Dunstan Pyle: Pyle's pitch. Boiled here forty years. You've sailed on it, likely. Every hull out of Reedwake's tarred with it.
Dunstan Pyle: Including the black ones. The census boats. I knew what they were. You boil pitch long enough, you stop asking what floats on it.

Dunstan Pyle: Word came up the coast that the isle's gone quiet and the beam's out. Two days later soldiers walked in from the west with a paper and wanted my whole stock. I said I'd have to see their money. They said they'd be back tonight with more men, and see mine.
Dunstan Pyle: I've a feeling you're the one the coast is talking about. I'd like them not to have it.
Dunstan Pyle: Their camp's out past the sinking ground. Don't step on anything that shines.
1. Find the soldiers' camp past the sinking ground
2. Stop Sergeant Tull taking Pyle's pitch for the census boats
3. Tell Dunstan Pyle his pitch is his own
Find the soldiers' camp past the sinking ground
"A soldiers' camp, made in a hurry, crown blue on everything. Tar barrels already stacked, Pyle's mark burned in their lids."

"An order sheet under a helmet: 'The isle is lost. The census continues. Requisition pitch from Pyle's yard, by force if required, for the refit of the Reedwake boats. Collection to resume by sea before the summer list.'"
"At the bottom, a seal, and the same neat hand as every receipt."
You: They've lost the isle, and the first thing they've thought of is how to start again.
Tell Dunstan Pyle his pitch is his own
Dunstan Pyle: Is it done? I heard it from here.
You: It's done. They had orders. The census goes on, they said - by sea, in boats tarred with your pitch.
Dunstan Pyle: With my pitch. Course with my pitch. Whose else?
Dunstan Pyle: Forty years I've told myself somebody'd have boiled it if I didn't. Which is true, and doesn't help.

Dunstan Pyle: I'll tell you what I'm going to do. I'm going to sell every barrel I've got to the Reedwake fishing boats, at cost, before anyone in blue comes asking again. Then I'll boil more and do it again.
Dunstan Pyle: Take this. Go easy - it's sticky.
Dunstan Pyle: The fishers came for the pitch. One of them shook my hand. Forty years, and nobody's shaken my hand.
Dunstan Pyle: I burned the old order book. It took all evening. Tarred pages burn slow.
: The census means to carry on by sea? Course it does. You don't stop a mill by breaking one wheel. So break the next one too.
Ash Is Somebody is a side quest, asked by Grisel Ombry (ash-sweeper). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Grisel Ombry: We bury the ash here. You'll think that's mad. Everyone from outside does.

Grisel Ombry: Not the black ash off the mountain - that's just mountain. The pale ash. The fine stuff that comes up through the cracks on a warm wind, grey and soft as flour. My mother said never sweep that into the river. That's somebody, she said.
Grisel Ombry: We wrap it in cloth like a body and put it under a stone. The old folk did, and I do, and the young ones laugh. Lately it's coming up in drifts. Some nights the drifts get up and walk.
Grisel Ombry: Put the walkers down first. They don't mean it. Then bring me cloth for the wrapping.
1. Put down 4 of the walkers that rise out of the ash drifts
2. Bring Grisel Ombry 4 cloth to wrap the pale ash
Bring Grisel Ombry 4 cloth to wrap the pale ash
Grisel Ombry: Good cloth. That'll wrap a good many.
Grisel Ombry: You've a face on you. Like you know something about the ash.
You: I've been under the ground. There's a road down there, and a furnace at the end of it. The crown's been feeding it people.
Grisel Ombry: Then my mother was right, and her mother. It's somebody. All of it's somebody.
Grisel Ombry: I'll not tell the young ones. Let them laugh. But I'll wrap every handful till I'm too old to bend, and then I'll teach one of them, and I won't say why.
Grisel Ombry: Forty-three bundles this month. I've stopped counting them as ash. I count them as people. It's quicker to cry that way, and then be done.
Grisel Ombry: The drifts have stopped walking. I like to think it's because someone's seeing to them.
: They wrap the ash out there like a body? Good. Somebody should. Somebody should have all along.
The Blue Door is a side quest, asked by Tobias Gell (back from below). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Tobias Gell: You'll not know me. I knew you, down there. You came past the pens with a lantern. I was the one asleep standing up.

Tobias Gell: I dug sulfur on these flats twenty years before the bell. The air below stank like this every hour of every day, and I hated it - and when the gates opened I walked straight here, because it's the only air that smells like home.
Tobias Gell: My wife's in our old house on the far side of the flats. Annet. Eight years. I've stood at the edge of the yellow three times and turned back.
Tobias Gell: Would you go first? Tell her I'm alive. Then come and tell me her face.
Tobias Gell: The house with the blue door. It'll still be blue. She painted it every spring, she was mad for it.
1. Tell Annet Gell that her husband is alive
2. Tell Tobias Gell his wife's face
Tell Annet Gell that her husband is alive
They: Tobias? Tobias is in the city. They gave me a paper. He went to serve in the king's kitchens.
You: There's no kitchen. He was below, under the ground. He's back. He's at the edge of the flats.
They: I married Wat Cobb. Four years ago. The man who bought Tobias's barrow. He's a good man. He's very kind to the goats.
They: I painted the door every spring. I don't know who for. I think I knew the paper was a lie, and I painted the door anyway.
They: Tell him to come. Tell him Wat will put the kettle on. Tell him I don't know what happens after that, and nor does he, and that's all right.
Tell Tobias Gell his wife's face
Tobias Gell: Well? Her face. Tell me her face.
You: She'd been told you were serving in the king's kitchens. She married Wat Cobb, four years ago.
Tobias Gell: Wat Cobb. Who bought my barrow.
Tobias Gell: ...He was always good with the goats.
You: She kept the door blue. Every spring. She says come. She says Wat will put the kettle on.
Tobias Gell: The door's still blue.

Tobias Gell: All right. I'll go. I'll stand in the yard and drink Wat Cobb's tea and we'll all look at each other. That's more than I had a month ago. Here - it's the only thing I brought up with me. I want rid of it.
Tobias Gell: Wat and me dug a new pit together yesterday. He's useless with a pick. Very good with the goats.
Tobias Gell: She still paints the door. She says it's for both of us now. I don't know what that means. I'm letting it mean something.
: A man walked home from down there and found his wife married again. ...Edrin never had a wife. That's one thing, I suppose.
Our Plaster is a side quest, asked by Hollin Pruett (plaster-burner). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.

Hollin Pruett: See the dunes? White as milk. That's gypsum. Burn it and grind it and you've plaster. My family's yard burned it two hundred years, and every scrap went up to the city on the crown's carts.
Hollin Pruett: They told us the city was white because the king was pure. It was white because of us. Four generations with burnt hands.

Hollin Pruett: Now bits of it are lying in our own dunes. I want to know if any of it's ours. Every block from Pruett's yard had a hand pressed in it before it set. My great-grandmother's, my grandad's, mine.
Hollin Pruett: Trouble is, some of the king's guard came down with it, and they're still marching about the wreck like there's a king to march for.
Hollin Pruett: Out where the big white piece came down - you'll see the gold on it from the ridge. Mind the guard. Nobody's told them.
1. Drive off 4 of the king's guard still holding the wreck
2. Look at the back of the fallen wall in the dunes
3. Tell Hollin Pruett whose hand was in the plaster
Look at the back of the fallen wall in the dunes
"A wall of white plaster the size of a barn, face-down in the white sand. Gold trim along one edge, blue cloth caught under it."

"Where it broke, the back of the plaster shows: rough, unpainted, and pressed into it while it was wet, the print of a hand. A small hand, with a crooked little finger. Beside it, scratched with a nail: P. YARD. 214."
"The front, the side the city saw, is smooth and white and says nothing at all."
You: Two hundred years of hands, and they faced them inwards.
Tell Hollin Pruett whose hand was in the plaster
You: Pruett's yard, year 214. A small hand, with a crooked little finger.
Hollin Pruett: ...My great-grandmother broke that finger in the kiln door. We all know that finger. It's on the yard gate.
Hollin Pruett: She went up there, then. On every wall. And now she's come home.
Hollin Pruett: I'll not burn plaster for anyone else again. Walls for people down here, with the hands on the outside, where you can see them.
Hollin Pruett: I've set her piece in the yard gate, the one with the hand. Facing out.
Hollin Pruett: People from the city keep coming asking for work. I tell them they'll burn their hands. They say good.
: The city was white because of a man's granny? I thought it was the clouds.
Old Gullet is a side quest, asked by Tansy Brack (eel-catcher). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Tansy Brack: Eel-traps. Willow, the long kind, with the funnel. I set forty a night along the cut and I've done it since I was nine.
Tansy Brack: This month I lift them and they're split down the side like a pea-pod. No eels. Bait gone. Once the whole trap went, rope and stake and all.
Tansy Brack: My dad would've said it was Old Gullet. Every bayou's got one. Something that gets big eating what other people catch.
Tansy Brack: I don't believe in Old Gullet. But something's eating my winter, and I'd like it to stop.
Tansy Brack: Down the cut, past the dead cypress with the rope on it. Go at dusk. It's punctual, I'll give it that.
1. Kill whatever's been splitting Tansy's eel-traps
2. Tell Tansy Brack her traps are safe
Tell Tansy Brack her traps are safe
Tansy Brack: Well? Was it Old Gullet?
You: It was something big that eats other people's catch. Call it what you like.
Tansy Brack: Old Gullet, then. Dad'll be insufferable, and he's been dead six years.
Tansy Brack: Did you open it? You're meant to. Old Gullet's belly is where you find what you lost.
You: Two of your trap-hooks. And this. A spoon.
Tansy Brack: ...That's silver. That's a crest on it. That came down the chutes from up there, into the water, into that, and now it's in my hand.
Tansy Brack: Forty years I've eaten off wood. Keep the spoon. Have some eels. I'll not eat with anything of theirs.
Tansy Brack: Forty traps, forty eels. Near enough. The bayou's back to being only mildly against me.
Tansy Brack: Dad always said Old Gullet would be the death of somebody. He never said whose.
: A silver spoon out of a beast's gut in the bayou. Up there they throw the cutlery away. Down here I mend the same pot nine times.
The Magpie Crabs is a side quest, asked by Lowri Penhallow (pearl diver, retired). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Lowri Penhallow: I dived this lagoon fifty years. Ears gone, chest gone. I can hold my breath about as long as it takes to complain. So now I open shells and dry the pearls on the flat rocks.
Lowri Penhallow: And the crabs take them. Not to eat. Crabs don't eat pearls. They carry them off and sit on them, like old men with a purse.
Lowri Penhallow: Every diver here will tell you the crabs are the drowned, still pearling. I'll tell you they're crabs, and I'd like five fewer of them.
You: I'll see to the crabs.
Lowri Penhallow: On the drying rocks and down the tideline. Don't let them nip you - they hold on out of spite.
1. Kill 5 crabs along Lowri's drying rocks
2. Tell Lowri Penhallow her pearls are safe
Tell Lowri Penhallow her pearls are safe
Lowri Penhallow: Five. I counted them going quiet.
Lowri Penhallow: Here's a thing nobody says out loud. When the crown's pearl-buyer comes round, he grades every pearl 'seconds' and pays seconds. Then they go up to the city as firsts.
Lowri Penhallow: So honestly, I'd rather the crabs had them. At least the crabs are open about it.
Lowri Penhallow: Take these. They're firsts. Don't let anybody with a seal on his coat tell you different.
Lowri Penhallow: The rocks are mine again. I sit with my feet in the water and nobody carries anything off.
Lowri Penhallow: Fifty years and I never once saw what they did with them up there. Buttons. It'll be buttons.
Pitcher Brandy is a side quest, asked by Ambrose Kell (fen-doctor). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Ambrose Kell: You've a cough. No? You will. Everybody in the fen has a cough by the first frost, and the cure is pitcher brandy.
Ambrose Kell: You take the water from inside a pitcher plant - the old ones, the big ones - and you steep berries in it, and then brandy, and then you sit by the fire and stop minding.
Ambrose Kell: The trouble is the big pitchers. There's one out on the black bog we call the Bishop. Tall as a child and twice as hungry. Best water in the fen. My knees won't take the bog.
Ambrose Kell: Don't fall in it. I mean that plainly. We lost a goat. Mind you, the batch that year was exceptional.
1. Draw water from the Bishop, the great pitcher plant on the black bog
2. Bring Ambrose Kell 4 handfuls of berries for the steeping
Draw water from the Bishop, the great pitcher plant on the black bog
"A pitcher plant as tall as a child, its throat speckled red like the inside of a mouth. It smells sweet and wrong."
"Inside, a pint of clear water. At the bottom, a tidy heap of bones - a vole, a bird, a great many beetles, and one goat's horn."
Bring Ambrose Kell 4 handfuls of berries for the steeping
Ambrose Kell: Oh, that's a good colour. That's Bishop water all right.
Ambrose Kell: And berries. Bog berries are best, but any will do. Between us, it's the brandy doing most of the work.
You: Then what's the pitcher water for?
Ambrose Kell: It makes people believe it's medicine. Believing is half of medicine. The brandy's the other half.
Ambrose Kell: Here. Last year's. For the cough you haven't got.
Ambrose Kell: How's the cough? Told you. Prevention.
Ambrose Kell: A crate of the city's physic came down the chutes once. Pretty bottles, gold seals. Water and sugar. So they're no better than me, and I've got brandy.
: Pitcher brandy. It's mostly brandy. Still, pitcher water does settle a sour stomach. Don't you dare tell him I said so.
Where the Water Goes is a side quest, asked by Senna Lowe (fog-net weaver). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.

Senna Lowe: Mind the nets. They're finer than they look. We hang them between the trees, the fog combs itself out on them and drips into the troughs. That's the village's water. All of it. There's no spring up here.
Senna Lowe: Spiders have got into the high nets. They like the fine mesh. Once they're in they spin over it, and the fog runs off their silk instead of ours and drips on the ground.
