Senna Lowe: Clear them out, bring me fibre to re-string what they've ruined, and I'll tell you a thing about the fog you won't believe.
Senna Lowe: The high nets, up the ridge. Watch your head. They drop when they're cross.
1. Clear 4 spiders out of the fog-nets
2. Bring Senna Lowe 5 fibre to re-string the nets
3. Tell Pip where the city's waterfalls end up
Bring Senna Lowe 5 fibre to re-string the nets
Senna Lowe: That'll string three nets. Good.
Senna Lowe: Now, the thing. Where do you think the fog comes from? Not the sea. The wind's wrong for the sea.

Senna Lowe: It's the city. The waterfalls off Crownreach. They never reach the ground, everyone knows that. They come apart on the way down, finer and finer, and the wind brings what's left here, and it combs out on my nets.
Senna Lowe: My grandmother tasted it and said it tasted of a long way down. She was a poet. It tastes of water.
You: So the waterfalls do reach the ground. Just not all at once.
Senna Lowe: If you know a child who'd want to know that, tell them. Children always ask.
Tell Pip where the city's waterfalls end up
You: Pip. You asked if the waterfalls reach the ground.
They: They don't. Tomas says they don't. He says they turn into nothing.
You: They turn into fog. It blows a long way and settles on a forest up a mountain, and people catch it in nets and drink it.
They: ...So it does get down. It just goes slow.
They: I'm going to drink some one day. I'm going to go there and drink the city.
Senna Lowe: The nets are full every morning. Whatever it was up there, it's ours now.
Senna Lowe: Did you tell the child? Good. Somebody ought to get a straight answer about that city.
: Pip says she's going to drink the city. Thanks for that. She won't touch the well now unless I call it fog water.

i: Brother Aubin, keeper of the lotus shrine
s: The Extra Lamp is a side quest, asked by Brother Aubin (keeper of the lotus shrine). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.

Brother Aubin: Every new moon the village floats lamps on the lotus water, one for each of our dead. I count them out and I count them back. The current turns at the shrine and brings them round to the reeds, and I fish them out and dry the wicks.
Brother Aubin: Thirty-one out, last month. Thirty-two came back.

Brother Aubin: I'm a monk, not a fool. Somebody's floating one from further up the marsh, where I can't see. And somebody who mourns in the dark doesn't want to be seen. I'd like to know why. And I'd like them to know they're welcome.
You: I'll find where it comes from.
Brother Aubin: Upstream, through the lotus. Look for a lamp that's still lit - the extra one is always the last to go out.
1. Find the extra lamp still burning up the lotus marsh
Find the extra lamp still burning up the lotus marsh
"A clay lamp, still lit, caught in the lotus roots. A twist of paper is tucked under the rim, kept dry with wax."
"For Corran, who the bell took at the turn of the year. Who volunteered, says the paper with the seal. I'm not to cry for a volunteer. They say it shames the list. So I'm crying out here."
"Below, in a smaller, rounder hand: AND ME FOR DA."
You: A woman and a child, mourning where nobody from the list can see.
They: If you've come about the lamp, I'll stop. I'll stop. Don't tell the reeve.
You: Brother Aubin sent me. He counts the lamps. He says yours is welcome on the shrine water with the others.
They: With the others? In front of everyone? When the paper says Corran went off keen as mustard?
They: The reeve says grieving a volunteer looks like calling the census a liar. And the next list's a long one.
You: Then let the list see thirty-two lamps.
They: ...Tell the Brother, next new moon. Me and the boy. We'll float it from the shrine like everybody else, and the reeve can write that down if he likes.
Brother Aubin: Thirty-two out, thirty-two back. And a boy holding the taper, very solemn, with the whole village watching.
Brother Aubin: The reeve came. He stood at the back and didn't write anything. That's a start.
: Not allowed to grieve a volunteer. Of course they aren't. That's what the receipt is for.
The Drowned Milestone is a side quest, asked by Jessamy Reed (punt-woman). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Jessamy Reed: There's a road under this water. A proper one, a royal road, paved. You can feel the stones with the pole on a still day.
Jessamy Reed: My granny said her granny walked it, before the Reckoning. She said it went to a city, and you could get there in four days with a donkey.
Jessamy Reed: At the lowest water there's a milestone stands out of the mud by the big dead oak. Nobody in my family reads. I want to know what it says before I die and it goes back to being a rock.
Jessamy Reed: Trouble is the crocodiles. They lie up in the roots there, and they're not shy.
You: I'll clear the way and read it.
Jessamy Reed: Kill a few and the rest get the idea. Then go to the dead oak at low water.
1. Kill 3 crocodiles in the drowned roots
2. Read the milestone by the big dead oak
3. Tell Jessamy Reed what the milestone says
Read the milestone by the big dead oak
"A square stone, green to the shoulders, crusted with snails. The road runs past it under the water, straight as a rule. A gold mark is set in its face, the paint gone to a stain."
"Cut in plain capitals: THE CROWN - IV LEAGUES. And under it, the royal mark: THE KING'S PEACE ON THIS ROAD."
"The road points the way the maps call the Hollow Crown. Four leagues on there's nothing but the edge of the chasm, and the city hanging over it."
You: Four days with a donkey. Then it went up, and left a hole, and the road walks straight into it.
Tell Jessamy Reed what the milestone says
Jessamy Reed: Well? What's it say?
You: 'The Crown, four leagues. The king's peace on this road.' It points at the chasm.
Jessamy Reed: Four days with a donkey. Granny's granny had a donkey called Patience. I always knew that and never knew why I knew it.
Jessamy Reed: So she walked to the city, on the ground, like going to market. And then one day there was a hole where it was, and the city up in the sky, and the road filling with water behind her.
Jessamy Reed: We say 'the Reckoning' like it was weather. Nobody says somebody did it.
Jessamy Reed: Here. It was Granny's. She said it was for the road.
Jessamy Reed: I punted out and put my hand on it. Four leagues. I said it out loud, so it had been said.
Jessamy Reed: My granddaughter's learning her letters now. I told her she has to. Rocks forget.
: Tomas says you found a sign that says the city used to be on the ground. Did people walk to it? Could I have?
Light Ballast is a side quest, asked by Jory Tallow (boatwright). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Jory Tallow: I caulk boats. Pitch and oakum, mallet and iron. Nine years I've done the crown's census boats out of Reedwake, and they pay in coin that rings, which is more than anyone else does.
Jory Tallow: A boat goes out to the isle sitting low, loaded to the strakes. It comes back riding so high it skates. Every time. I have to put stones in her so she sits right on the slip.
Jory Tallow: Servants for the city, they say. Fine. But she comes back empty of everything. No water casks for passengers. No bread, no buckets. Nobody's planning for anyone to ride back.
Jory Tallow: The boatmen keep a tally-bag. Old Dunnock lost his in the mangroves when he went over drunk. Find it, and I'd like to see the sticks.
Jory Tallow: Where the channel bends through the roots. He went in by a dead stump with a boat-hook still stuck in it.
1. Find the boatman's tally-bag lost in the mangroves
Find the boatman's tally-bag lost in the mangroves
"A tarred leather bag wedged in the roots, sodden. Inside, a bundle of hazel sticks tied with twine, each one notched and burned with a date."
"Every stick has two faces. OUT, with notches - forty, thirty-eight, forty-two. BACK, smooth. Not one notch on the back of any stick."
"One has a third mark, burned small near the end: ONE OVER THE SIDE, MID-STRAIT. NOT RECOVERED."
You: Nine years of sticks and not one notch for coming back. The only one who got off that boat did it in the middle of the strait.
Jory Tallow: ...Out, out, out. Back, nothing. Nine years, and I've been greasing the slip for it.
Jory Tallow: No. Servants, they say. Servants get a day off, don't they? Servants come home for a wedding.
Jory Tallow: There's a hull on the slip for them now. I'll finish her, because they'll hang me if I don't. But I'll do it slow. And I'm going to think about what else a man who caulks boats could do.
Jory Tallow: She's on the slip. I'm caulking her very carefully. Very, very slowly.
Jory Tallow: Dunnock wanted his sticks back. I told him the mangroves had them. Which they did, for a while.
: A caulker who did the census boats? I did the wheels on the cages. We should sit down sometime, him and me, and not say anything.

Quest(52).t: A Skiff for the Other Way
s: A Skiff for the Other Way is a side quest, asked by Jory Tallow (boatwright). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Jory Tallow: I'm not doing the crown's boats any more. Told the boatmaster my back's gone. It isn't. I've been building these.
Jory Tallow: Flat skiffs. Draw a hand's depth of water, no more. You can pole one through the bayou channels where no crown boat will ever float, all the way up the coast.
Jory Tallow: Sera Quill's people run them. A family hears their name's on the next list, they're in a skiff the night before the bell, and the collectors find an empty house and a pot still warm.
Jory Tallow: I need planks for the next two. Then the chart wants taking to Quill's channel-pilot. I won't go myself. Too many people know my face round the landing.
Jory Tallow: Six good planks. Then I'll give you the chart. Don't fold it - it's on calfskin, it cracks.
1. Bring Jory Tallow 6 planks for the skiffs
2. Take Jory's chart to Dace, Sera Quill's channel-pilot
Bring Jory Tallow 6 planks for the skiffs
Jory Tallow: Straight grain. Good. That's two hulls.
Jory Tallow: Here's the chart. Every channel through the roots that'll take a hand of water at the ebb. Fifteen years of mending boats for men who talk while they wait.
Jory Tallow: Dace runs the landing on the far side of the reeds. Give it to her and nobody else. If anyone else asks, you're lost and looking for eels.
Take Jory's chart to Dace, Sera Quill's channel-pilot
They: You've got eel-hunter written all over you. Badly.
You: Jory Tallow sent this. Don't fold it.
They: ...Oh, that's beautiful. That's the Withy Cut. I didn't know the Withy Cut took a boat at all.
They: Do you know what this is? Two more families a month, up the coast, past the toll forts, where the list doesn't reach. Sera will want to kiss him. Tell him to brace.
They: And you. If you're ever going over to the isle, come to Reedwake and ask for Quill. You'll want someone who knows the ebb.
Jory Tallow: Two hulls in the water. Turns out a man sleeps better building the right boat.
Jory Tallow: Dace sent word. The Withy Cut takes a boat. She says thank you, and something else I won't repeat.
: A boat that goes the other way, the night before the bell. If I'd known, back when the list came... No. I'd have stayed. Somebody has to carry Aunt Mara's baskets.

i: A Skiff for the Other Way
s: Riding Low is a side quest, asked by Jory Tallow (boatwright). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Jory Tallow: The beam over the spire's dark. Word came the night after. Since then Dace has been taking skiffs over at the ebb and bringing people back off the isle. Off it. The other way.
Jory Tallow: Seven boatloads. Thin as rakes, the lot of them, but alive. I've never been so glad to see a boat ride low.
Jory Tallow: The eighth hasn't come in. Dace herself, with five off the isle. Two nights late. There's a mangrove key out at the channel mouth she'd lie up on if the tide turned on her.
Jory Tallow: And there's wreckers on that shore. The Gannets. They strip whatever comes ashore, and they don't wait for it to be dead.
Jory Tallow: The key at the channel mouth. Look for a fire. Dace always makes a fire, she hates being wet.
1. Find where Dace's skiff put in on the mangrove key
2. Deal with Hake Gannet and get Dace's people back
3. Bring Dace and the five back to Jory Tallow
Find where Dace's skiff put in on the mangrove key
"A cold fire, a lean-to of oars and sailcloth, the skiff dragged into the roots with its bottom stove in. Footprints everywhere - bare ones, and boots."
"On the thwart, scratched with a knife: GANNETS. TAKING US NORTH ALONG THE SHORE. THEY THINK ISLE PEOPLE ARE WORTH SOMETHING TO SOMEBODY. D."
You: Wreckers who heard the crown pays for people. Of course they did.
Bring Dace and the five back to Jory Tallow
Jory Tallow: You've brought them. All of them? Count them for me. I can't, my hands are going.
You: Dace and five. Hake Gannet won't be selling anyone.
Jory Tallow: He meant to sell them back. To whoever's buying, now the isle's gone quiet. There's always a buyer for people, if you're the kind who looks for one.
Jory Tallow: Dace says the skiff's firewood. I'll build her another. I'll build her ten.
Jory Tallow: I used to ballast the crown's boats with stones so they'd sit right coming home. Look at that one. Riding low with people. That's how a boat's meant to sit.
Jory Tallow: Ten skiffs, I said, and I meant it. Nobody's paying a penny, and I've never been so well off.
Jory Tallow: One of the five asked if I was the man who caulked the census boats. I said yes. She said, 'Well, you've caulked this one,' and that was all.
: People coming off the isle by skiff, at the ebb? Send any that need a bed this way. Nobody at Briar's Rest asks questions with their mouth full.
The Tide Cairns is a side quest, asked by Merrin Sollas (cockle-picker). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.

Merrin Sollas: At the spring ebb the sea goes out a mile and a half. You can walk to the outer banks for cockles if you know the way, and the way is the cairns. White stone on the sea side, so you know which way you're facing when the fog comes.

Merrin Sollas: Somebody's been moving them. Last week my girl followed the line out, and the line went into the soft sand by the Gut, and the sea came back faster than a horse. She's alive because she can swim. Most of us can't.
Merrin Sollas: I want to know who. Look at the cairns past the stake-nets. You'll see which ones are wrong.
You: I'll look at the cairns.
Merrin Sollas: Past the stake-nets. Go on the ebb and be back before the turn. I mean that.
1. Look at the tide cairns past the stake-nets
2. Find where the true line of cairns used to run
3. Tell Merrin Sollas who moved the cairns
Look at the tide cairns past the stake-nets
"A knee-high cairn of beach stones with the white one set on top. On the wrong side - turned toward the land, so a walker would think the sea was behind them."
"The weed on the stones is on their dry faces. Moved, and lately. Pressed into the sand beside it, a boot-heel with a nail pattern: three and a cross."
You: Somebody turned the line on purpose. Toward the Gut.
Find where the true line of cairns used to run
"The true cairn's been pulled down and scattered. In among the stones, sodden: a blue cloth armband with a gold mark. A crown rider's."
"And a scrap of oilcloth, in a fast hand: CENSUS RIDERS CUT ACROSS THE FLATS FROM THE TOLL ROAD TO TAKE THE LISTED OFF THE BANKS. TURN THE CAIRNS ON RIDER NIGHTS. - Q."
You: Q. Sera Quill's crews. They turned the cairns to drown the census riders. And nearly drowned a cockler's girl.
Tell Merrin Sollas who moved the cairns
You: Quill's crews moved them. The census riders cut across the flats to take people off the banks. Your cairns have drowned at least one of them.
Merrin Sollas: They took my brother off those banks two winters ago, with his rake still in his hand. Riders came out of the fog.
Merrin Sollas: So I'm meant to be glad. And I am. And my girl went into the Gut.

Merrin Sollas: I'll build the true line again myself. And I'll build a wrong one beside it for rider nights, and teach every child on this shore which is which. That's what it's come to. Children learning two sets of cairns.
Merrin Sollas: Two lines now. White stone seaward on the true one, white stone on the left on the other. The children had it in an afternoon. They're quicker than us.
Merrin Sollas: If you see Quill, tell her a cockler's girl nearly paid for her riders. She'll know. I'd just like her to know it twice.
: Drowning riders with cairns. I'd have done the same. I'd have told the cocklers first, though.

i: Teague Holloway, back from Saint Orra's
s: Marks on the Pile is a side quest, asked by Teague Holloway (back from Saint Orra's). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Teague Holloway: I was in the cells on Saint Orra's. Three years. You were the one with the key. I'll not forget your face, though I'd like to forget the rest.
Teague Holloway: I rowed home. The house is there, up on its legs over the water. Empty. Ladder pulled up, door tied shut with a reed-knot. My wife's knot.
Teague Holloway: Every house here marks the children on the corner pile, by the ladder - a notch each midsummer. I've two girls. I want to know how far up the marks go before they stop.
Teague Holloway: I can't make myself climb down and look. If they stop the year I left... I'd sooner somebody else saw it first.
You: I'll look at the pile.
Teague Holloway: The house with the blue rag on the gutter. Corner pile, by the ladder. Low tide's best.
1. Look at the height marks on the corner pile of Teague's house
2. Tell Teague Holloway what the pile says
3. Find Wyn Holloway at Sallow Key and tell her Teague is coming
Look at the height marks on the corner pile of Teague's house
"A mangrove pile thick as a thigh, notched up one face in two rows. Beside each notch a letter: B on the left, M on the right."
"The notches climb in short steps, the same each year. Then three more pairs in a different hand, cut deeper - a knife, not a chisel. They don't stop."
"The last pair is fresh, the sap still in the cut. Beside them, scratched small: GONE TO SALLOW KEY. B AND M AND ME."
You: They kept marking. They grew. And she left word where they went.
Tell Teague Holloway what the pile says
Teague Holloway: Well? Say it quick.
You: The marks don't stop. Three more years, in another hand, and the last pair's fresh. She cut 'Gone to Sallow Key' beside them.
Teague Holloway: Sallow Key. Her mother's lot.
Teague Holloway: Three years taller. Bryony'll be up to my chest.
Teague Holloway: Go on ahead of me. Tell Wyn I'm coming. If I walk in out of the water after three years, she'll take the boat-hook to me. She'll think I'm a drowned man come back for his supper.
Find Wyn Holloway at Sallow Key and tell her Teague is coming
They: You're not from the Key. Mind the third rung, it's rotten.
You: Teague's alive. He was in the cells on Saint Orra's. He's back at the old house, and he sent me first.
They: I cut his mark every midsummer too. Round the back of the pile, where the girls wouldn't see. Same height every year. I didn't know why I did it. You don't grow when you're dead.
They: Tell him the ladder's down. And tell him not to come by water - I'll take the boat-hook to anything that climbs out of the water at night. He can come by the path like a man.
Teague Holloway: She made me come by the path. Then she hit me with the boat-hook anyway. Gently.
Teague Holloway: Bryony's to my chest. Moll's past it. I missed the bit in between and I'm not missing any more.
: A man home from the isle, and his wife kept cutting his height on the house-post? Every year, the same height? ...Give me a minute.
The Breathing Sinkhole is a side quest, asked by Beck Oriel (karst guide). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Beck Oriel: You've been down. I can see it. People who've been under the ground stand like the roof's still on them.
Beck Oriel: This land's all holes. Sinkholes, wells, drops into the dark you could lose a village in. We've always known some go a long way. Water goes in and never comes back up.
Beck Oriel: This year one of them started breathing out. Warm air, smelling of smoke and hot iron. And a bell down there, ringing on its own. You'll know that bell.
Beck Oriel: Now there's people camped at the lip in black, lowering baskets on ropes at night. Big baskets. Somebody's goat went first. Then the Tull lad.
Beck Oriel: Through the fig gate and down the gully. Follow the warm air. Go armed.
1. Find the sinkhole that breathes warm air
2. Stop Deacon Orme Calloway lowering people into the sinkhole
3. Tell Beck Oriel the sinkhole's keepers are done
Find the sinkhole that breathes warm air

"A shrine built new at the lip of the drop, of stacked limestone. On it the royal census mark, painted fresh in gold, and under it the other mark - the one from the gateway below. Copied carefully, from somewhere."
"A rope runs over a worn log into the dark, taut with weight. A slate leans on the shrine: TITHE OF THE FAITHFUL. HE COUNTS. HE REMEMBERS WHO PAID EARLY."
"Warm air comes up out of the dark. Far down, the bell keeps no time at all."
You: They're paying his debt for him, out of their own neighbours. Hoping to be remembered when he comes to collect.
Tell Beck Oriel the sinkhole's keepers are done
Beck Oriel: You came back up the gully. Did they?
You: No. There was weight on the rope. I hauled it up. The Tull lad, tied in a basket, cold and furious.
Beck Oriel: Furious is good. Furious is alive.
Beck Oriel: Calloway was a tithe-reeve, you know. Thirty years he filled the crown's crates. Then he heard where the crates were really going, and decided he'd rather be on the side that eats.
Beck Oriel: I'll pull the shrine down and roll the stones in after it. Let the hole breathe on its own. Nobody here is paying anybody early.
Beck Oriel: The shrine's in the hole. The air still comes up warm some nights. We've put a fence round it and a sign in plain words.
Beck Oriel: The Tull lad tells everyone he fought them off himself. Let him. It's a better story than the other one.
: A sinkhole with that bell under it? Same as the Last Vein. That whole country's got holes in it going to the same place.
Good Hands is a side quest, asked by Ottilie Brisk (raft-woman). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.

Ottilie Brisk: When the city came down, a piece of it came into my lake. A whole wall, white plaster, gold edging, floating like a door. There was a man on it, holding on by his fingernails. He can't swim. Nobody up there could, he says.
Ottilie Brisk: He's in my hut. Lammas, he's called. Polite. Eats like a heron. Says he was a clerk in some office, and won't say which.
Ottilie Brisk: His box went down with the wall, out by the lily islands. He cries about it in his sleep. Bring it up, and maybe he'll tell me what he was. I'd like to know who I've got under my roof.
Ottilie Brisk: The white wall's still out there, past the lily islands, half sunk. You'll see the gold from the shore.
1. Search the fallen wall in the lake for Lammas's box
2. Show Lammas Pike what was in his box
3. Tell Ottilie Brisk what Lammas was
Search the fallen wall in the lake for Lammas's box
"A slab of white plaster with gold trim, a scrap of blue cloth still nailed to a batten. Wedged under it, a lacquered box, watertight."
"Inside: spools of linen thread, needles, a brass thimble worn thin. And tags - a hundred blank linen tags, each with one word already stitched in a small, neat hand. RECEIVED."
"A ledger page, pressed flat: TALLY OFFICE, SECOND BENCH. QUOTA ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY BEFORE THE NOON BELL."
You: Him, or the one on the bench beside him. Stitching the word before the names.
Show Lammas Pike what was in his box
They: You found it. Oh, you found it. The thimble was my mother's -
You: There are a hundred tags in here with RECEIVED on them. Before the names.

They: We were told it was a formality. A blessing on them. The names came later from the office downstairs, and we never saw them. A hundred and twenty a morning, thirty-one years. I was fast. They gave me a ribbon.
They: I never once wondered where 'received' was. Isn't that strange? Thirty-one years, and I never asked received by whom.
They: Will you tell her? Ottilie. I can't. She brought me soup.
Tell Ottilie Brisk what Lammas was
Ottilie Brisk: Well? What was he?
You: He stitched the census tags. The word RECEIVED, before the names went on. A hundred and twenty a morning, for thirty-one years.
Ottilie Brisk: My cousin went off in a cage with one of those on his wrist.
Ottilie Brisk: I could put him back on his wall and push it out into the lake. I thought about it the whole time you were talking.

Ottilie Brisk: But he's got good hands. Fast, neat. There's a hundred nets on this lake want mending and nobody to mend them since the bell took the menders. He can stitch something useful for thirty-one years. Then we'll talk.
Ottilie Brisk: He mends a net faster than anyone on the lake. He doesn't talk while he does it. Neither do I.
Ottilie Brisk: He asked me yesterday what my cousin's name was. I told him. He stitched it into the corner of the net he was on. Just the name. No other word.
: The man who stitched RECEIVED, mending nets on a lake. I want to hate him properly and I can't find the right size of it. Leave him to his nets.
Said Aloud is a side quest, asked by Ebba Thrale (spore-gatherer). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Ebba Thrale: You'll not have heard the rule, being new. Under the caps, you don't say your name. Not out loud. Not even to your mother.
Ebba Thrale: The hollows keep what you say. Cough, and the caps come up in a cough-shape. Say your name and they grow it - letters in the moss, bright as lamps.
Ebba Thrale: My grandson Perrin said his on a dare. Shouted it down the old cut, the little article. That was three nights ago.
Ebba Thrale: I'm too stiff for the cut. Go and see if it's took. If it has, I want every cap of it picked before somebody comes along who reads.
Ebba Thrale: Down the old cut, where it goes blue. And don't you say yours while you're there.
1. Find the place in the old cut where Perrin shouted his name
2. Kill 3 of the hollow's wild things drawn to the glowing name
3. Pick Perrin's name out of the moss and bring Ebba the caps (5 glowcaps)
Find the place in the old cut where Perrin shouted his name
"A ring of glowcaps on a bank of black moss, each the size of a thumb, all lit the same cold blue."
"Inside the ring they've come up in lines. Crude, but there's no mistaking it: PERRIN."
"Further along the bank, older rings, gone brown and slumped. A few letters still hold. ...LL. ...OBY. Beside each old ring, a row of short upright caps, like a tally."
"Beside Perrin's, the first two marks of a new row have just come up."
You: Somebody's counting the names this place keeps. Or something is.
Pick Perrin's name out of the moss and bring Ebba the caps (5 glowcaps)
Ebba Thrale: That's him? That's all of him?
You: P, E, two Rs, I, N. And a ring round it. And a little row of marks starting, like the ones beside the old names.
Ebba Thrale: Marks. My gran used to say the hollow tallies for somebody. I thought she said it to make us mind.
Ebba Thrale: Right. These go on the fire, and he goes on bread and water till he's learnt a different dare.
Ebba Thrale: Have a cap-lamp for your trouble. There's no name in it. I grew it quiet.
Ebba Thrale: Perrin's learnt to whisper. He whispers his name to himself in bed, to check it's still his.
Ebba Thrale: Nobody here signs anything. My gran wouldn't put her mark on a bill of sale. I'm starting to see her point.
: Is it true there's a place where if you say your name the mushrooms write it down? I said mine into a bucket to see. Nothing.

i: Hettie Moorcock, keeper of a bone orchard
s: The Heavy Years is a side quest, asked by Hettie Moorcock (keeper of a bone orchard). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Hettie Moorcock: Buttons, glue, needles, dice. Knife-handles in a big year. That's what a bone orchard's for, whatever they say about us in the valley.
Hettie Moorcock: The trees fruit at night. You hear them crack. And lately there's others come up to pick. Up out of the ground, without asking.
Hettie Moorcock: They don't eat it. They just carry it about between the rows. Clear them off for me, would you? I'm one woman with a hook.
Hettie Moorcock: Go at dusk, between the old rows. And on your way back, look at my gran's tally post at the top. I want to know if it's what I think it is.
1. Clear 4 of the dead that come up to pick in the bone orchard
2. Look at the tally post at the top of the orchard
3. Tell Hettie Moorcock what the tally post says
Look at the tally post at the top of the orchard
"A post of grey wood, worn smooth by hands, notched from the ground to higher than your head. A row for every year's harvest, cut with different knives."
"Most rows are short. Every so often there's one three times as long - a heavy year. Beside every heavy row someone has scratched a little bell."
"The last row is this year's. It's long already. Someone has begun a bell beside it, and not finished."
You: Heavy years and bells. The trees bear hardest in the years the census comes.
Tell Hettie Moorcock what the tally post says
Hettie Moorcock: Well? Are they heavy years, or are they bell years?
You: They're the same years. Every long row has a bell by it. This year's is half-cut.
Hettie Moorcock: My gran cut those bells. She never said why, and I never asked, because I knew.
Hettie Moorcock: I don't eat from the heavy years. I make buttons out of them. Buttons are for keeping things together.
Hettie Moorcock: Here. A hook, the good one. And dice, from a heavy year. Don't play for anything you'd mind losing.
Hettie Moorcock: Quiet at the top of the rows now. The trees still crack. I'd rather that than footsteps.
Hettie Moorcock: If you hear of a bell coming this way, tell me first. I'll want baskets.
: A bone orchard that bears heavy in census years. My mother wouldn't have a bone button in the house. I'm starting to think she knew something.

i: Gert Ormsby, headwoman of a rust hamlet
s: Where Iron Goes Soft is a side quest, asked by Gert Ormsby (headwoman of a rust hamlet). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Gert Ormsby: You'll have noticed your knife going orange. Leave it in the dust overnight and you'll have a handful of red flakes and a handle.

Gert Ormsby: That's why we live here. Nothing iron comes into the Rust and stays - not a cage, not a bell-frame, not a knight. The census hasn't come in thirty years. Four hamlets of us, all from somewhere else.
Gert Ormsby: Last week a banner went up at the edge of the Wastes. Blue and gold, on a pole that doesn't rust. And men with it in armour that doesn't either.
Gert Ormsby: I want to know what they've brought. And I want them gone before they find us.
Gert Ormsby: East, past the red stumps. Your buckle will go first, so don't wear a good one.
1. Find the census banner at the edge of the Rust Wastes
2. Drive off the collectors camped by the banner
3. Tell Gert Ormsby what the banner said
Find the census banner at the edge of the Rust Wastes
"A royal census banner on a pole of something pale and smooth that isn't wood and isn't iron. Not a speck of rust on it."
"Nailed to the pole, a notice under the royal seal: THE WASTES ARE RECLAIMED TO THE CENSUS. PERSONS FOUND HEREIN ARE PRESUMED VOLUNTEERS."
"Below, the names of four hamlets, in a neat hand. All four spelt right. Somebody told them."
You: Presumed volunteers. They don't even have to ask any more.
Tell Gert Ormsby what the banner said
Gert Ormsby: They're gone? All of them?
You: All of them. The notice says the Wastes are reclaimed to the census. It had your hamlets' names on it.
Gert Ormsby: All four. Spelt right.
Gert Ormsby: Then somebody here wrote to them. Somebody who wanted a name taken off a list somewhere else, and traded ours for it.
Gert Ormsby: I'll find out who. Quietly. Take this - it's bronze. Bronze is the one thing the Rust leaves alone.
Gert Ormsby: It was a man from the third hamlet. His sister's on a list at Wen's Cross. I can't even hate him properly.
Gert Ormsby: We took the pole down. Can't burn it, can't rust it. It's a washing line now.
: Armour that won't rust? I'd want to see that. Then I'd want to put it in the forge and find out what it's really made of.

i: Hollin Strake, census officer, off duty
s: Same Hand, Same Ink is a side quest, asked by Hollin Strake (census officer, off duty). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Hollin Strake: Don't look at me like that. I don't take anyone. I read the list. The knight does the taking. There's a difference, though I couldn't tell you what it is any more.
Hollin Strake: We carry the letter-post as well. A penny a letter, up to the city, for the ones who went. Six weeks later the replies come down with the next list, and I hand them out.
Hollin Strake: This round I dropped the reply sack. On purpose, if you want the truth. Under the culvert by the old milestone.
Hollin Strake: I want somebody who isn't me to open it. Read three. Any three. Then tell me I'm wrong.
Hollin Strake: The culvert by the milestone. Blue wax on the sack. Break it - I'll say a fox did it.
1. Find the reply sack Hollin dropped under the culvert
2. Take Aldo Pennick the reply addressed to him
3. Tell Hollin Strake what the replies say
Find the reply sack Hollin dropped under the culvert
"A mail sack sealed with blue wax and the royal mark. Inside, forty letters, folded alike, on the same good paper."
"'Dear Mother, I am well and the bread is white. The work is light and I see the sky. Do not trouble to write often. Your loving son.'"
"'Dear Father, I am well and the bread is white. The work is light and I see the sky. Do not trouble to write often. Your loving daughter.'"
"The third is the same. The hand is the same in all forty: small and neat, with long loops on the R."
Take Aldo Pennick the reply addressed to him
They: Is that the post? You're not the reader. Is there one for Pennick? From Liss?
You: There's one with your name on it.
They: ...'I am well and the bread is white.' She'd never say white. She'd say pale. She was particular.
They: And she wrote crooked. Uphill, always. This is straight as a rule.
They: Don't tell me anything else. I'll keep it. It's got her name on it. That's something, isn't it? That's something.
Tell Hollin Strake what the replies say
You: Forty letters, one hand, long loops on the R. I gave Aldo Pennick his. He knew it wasn't her.
Hollin Strake: They all know. They just haven't said it to each other yet.

Hollin Strake: I've a split lip from a lad at a waystation last spring who wouldn't go quiet in the line. Vale, his name was. I wrote 'volunteer' on his receipt, because the knight said the count had to come right.
Hollin Strake: I've been wondering whose hand his reply would be in. Now I know. Here - the post pennies. I'm not carrying them up.
Hollin Strake: I'm going to stop at the next posting-house and not get up again. Let them write me down for it.
Hollin Strake: Pennick came to find me. He brought me an egg. I don't know what to do with that.
: The officer who wrote 'volunteer' for Edrin. He knows he wrote it. That's something. Not much. Something.
: The letter-post rode up on the convoy carts. Little blue sacks under the driver's bench. I mended that bench.
Turning the Coat is a side quest, asked by Merriam Coe (a crossbowman, lately). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Merriam Coe: Don't reach for anything. I've a bow and I'm tired, and both of those make me careless.
Merriam Coe: Four of us walked out of the escort at the ford a fortnight back. They gave us a cage of children to march to the coast. I've marched worse. I couldn't march that.
Merriam Coe: Lennart was meant to meet us at the old charcoal camp. He hasn't. And there's a patrol out from the fort looking for its missing coats.
Merriam Coe: They don't hang deserters, you know. They put you on the list. Find out what happened to Len, and I'll owe you.
Merriam Coe: The charcoal camp, past the burnt hill. Tall, whistles badly. He'll have kept his tabard, because he's an idiot.
1. Find the charcoal camp where Lennart was meant to wait
2. Kill 4 of the crown's soldiers hunting the deserters
3. Bring Merriam Coe 3 cloth to cover the deserters' blue
Find the charcoal camp where Lennart was meant to wait
"A cold charcoal pit and a lean-to of branches. A blue tabard, folded square, weighed down with a stone."
"Scratched into the bark of the lean-to's pole with a knife point: MERRY - THEY HAD MY MOTHER'S NAME ON THE NEXT LIST. WENT BACK SO THEY'D TAKE IT OFF. DON'T COME. L."
You: He went back in, to keep his mother off the list.
Bring Merriam Coe 3 cloth to cover the deserters' blue
Merriam Coe: Len went back? For his mother?
Merriam Coe: ...Of course he did. And folded his tabard first. He was always folding things.
Merriam Coe: Cloth. Good. Brown, grey, anything but blue. We'll be wool-carders by Sunday, or drovers, or whatever's being hired.
Merriam Coe: Have the bolts. And the boots - soldiers' boots, resoled. They don't sound like soldiers any more. I checked.
Merriam Coe: Wool-carding is harder than soldiering. Nobody tells you that.
Merriam Coe: If you ever see Lennart in a line of blue coats, he's the one whistling badly. You'll know him.
: Deserters. Good. I'd still not turn my back on one. But good.

i: Linnet Garve, surveyor of the old royal roads
s: The Last Mile is a side quest, asked by Linnet Garve (surveyor of the old royal roads). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Linnet Garve: I measure roads. Measured them for the crown, back when the crown wanted roads measured. Now I measure them because nobody else is going to.
Linnet Garve: The old royal road comes at the Scar straight from the west. Milestones every mile, and then it runs into that, and I'd always assumed it stopped.
Linnet Garve: It doesn't. You can see the stones going on along the lip. And they're numbered wrong. Mile three, then mile two. Counting down. Towards what?
Linnet Garve: My knees won't do the edge. Read the faces, not the tops. The crown always cut the useful bit low.
Linnet Garve: Follow the road to the lip. Don't look down for long. People say it looks back, and I've never wanted to find out.
1. Read the milestone where the royal road meets the Void Scar
2. Find the last milestone along the lip of the Scar
3. Tell Linnet Garve what the milestones count down to
Read the milestone where the royal road meets the Void Scar
"A milestone, waist-high, the royal road's mark cut on the top. On the face: 3."
"Under the number, older and half-sanded away by someone who didn't finish the job: a sign that isn't any letter. Hooked, deliberate. The same sign that's on the seals of the old census rolls."
You: The road didn't stop at the Scar. It goes on. Down.
Find the last milestone along the lip of the Scar
"This one is lying on its face. Something heaved it over, or it was set that way on purpose."
"On the underside, against the dirt, where nobody walking the road would ever read it: 1. And the hooked sign again, cut deep. The chisel marks are still pale."
You: Fresh. Somebody's still keeping this road.
Tell Linnet Garve what the milestones count down to
Linnet Garve: Well. Three, and then?
You: Three, two, one. The one's face down, with the sign cut new. And under the three: 'to the gate'.
Linnet Garve: Which gate? There's no gate on any map I've ever drawn, and I've drawn all of them.
Linnet Garve: ...No. Don't guess for me. I'll put it on the map as I found it. 'To the gate. Distance, one mile. Direction - down.'
Linnet Garve: Take my second-best chain. A hundred links, every one true. Measure something honest with it.
Linnet Garve: I've drawn it in. A road with a mile to go and no end. It's the most honest map I've ever made.
Linnet Garve: If you ever find the gate, don't tell me the distance. I couldn't bear to have been right.
: A road that goes down, with the chisel marks still fresh? There was dressed stone going down under the Last Vein too. I didn't like that either.
The Giant's Wrist is a side quest, asked by Jessamy Coil (bone-carver). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Jessamy Coil: Giant bone carves like soft cheese for the first hour and like flint after. You have to be quick and you have to be sure. My mother was both. I'm quick.
Jessamy Coil: There's a wrist out past the great ribs I've wanted for years. Big as a cottage. Something's denned in the hand, though, and it doesn't share.
Jessamy Coil: Clear it for me and you can see what I've seen in that wrist. I've only had a glass on it from a distance, and I don't trust my glass.
Jessamy Coil: Out past the ribs, where the fingers stick up like fence posts. It feeds at noon. Don't go at noon.
1. Kill Old Knuckle, denned in the giant's hand
3. Tell Jessamy Coil what's in the wrist
"The wrist is as big as a cottage, grey-white, split along the grain."
"All the way round it, a groove has been worn deep and smooth - a hand's width, polished like a doorstep. Rust-brown in the bottom of it."
"A shackle wore that. A shackle the size of a cart-wheel, for longer than anything should be held."
"Inside the split, someone has scratched tallies into the marrow channel. Thousands of them, in fives. Then they stop."
You: It was chained. Whatever these were, somebody held them. And somebody counted.
Tell Jessamy Coil what's in the wrist
You: A shackle-groove round the whole wrist, worn smooth. Rust in it. And tallies inside the bone, thousands.
Jessamy Coil: The old ones here say the giants held up the sky before the city. Shouldered it, my nan said. Proud of them, she was.
Jessamy Coil: Nobody wears a groove like that holding something up. You get a groove like that pulling against something.
Jessamy Coil: I've carved you a head from the knuckle. Quick and sure. I've been practising sure.
Jessamy Coil: I don't carve from the wrists any more. Fingers only. Fingers didn't know.
Jessamy Coil: Somebody chained a giant before there was a kingdom to do it. Who? I keep asking the bone. It's a poor talker.
Surety is a side quest, asked by Wat Fennimore (crater-shepherd). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Wat Fennimore: Everything ends up in a crater. Rain, stones, goats. You learn to farm the bottom. Best soil there is - it's all what's fallen, rotted.

Wat Fennimore: The big crater's got a star in it. Fell the night the city went up, the old ones say. Grass won't grow round it. Gold lines come up on the ground there at dusk, in rings, and then a goat drops.
Wat Fennimore: Now there's a lot in white robes camped on the lip. The Starwatch. They sing at it and feed it - goats. My goats. They say it's waking up.
Wat Fennimore: I'd like somebody to look at it who isn't singing. Tell me what I'm looking at.
You: I'll look at your star.
Wat Fennimore: The big crater, the one with no grass. Don't stand in the gold. I couldn't tell you why. I just know.
1. Look at the star in the big crater
2. Drive the Starwatch away from the crater
3. Tell Wat Fennimore what his star is
Look at the star in the big crater
"It isn't a star. It's a block of dressed white stone, cracked down the middle, banded with gold - the same make as the ward stations on Saint Orra's Isle."
"Round it on the ground, faint gold rings written in tight script: the marks Severin drew where judgment was about to fall. They tighten as you watch, then fade."
"Cut in the stone's flank, a line of the old script. Under it, in plain letters, someone's careful translation: '...AND THE GROUND BENEATH SHALL STAND SURETY FOR THE CITY ABOVE.'"
You: A ward stone that came off the city when it rose. Still judging, after all this time. And somebody pledged the ground.
Tell Wat Fennimore what his star is
Wat Fennimore: Is it waking up?
You: It never went to sleep. It's a ward stone off the city - it fell when the city rose. It kills what comes too close, the way the city's ward does.
Wat Fennimore: Off the city. So it's the city's star. Course it is.
You: There's writing on it. 'The ground beneath shall stand surety for the city above.'
Wat Fennimore: Surety. That's what you put up for a loan when you've nothing else. My da put up the goats once.
Wat Fennimore: So we're the goats. Here - cheese, goat's. It's the one thing round here that's ours outright. And take his stick. He kept waving it at the stone as if it'd listen.
Wat Fennimore: I've built a wall round the gold. Goats can't read, but they can't climb either.
Wat Fennimore: Surety. I asked a priest. It's a word for something kept in case someone doesn't pay.
: Surety. That's a moneylender's word. I've heard it said to farmers at this table, the years the tribute came up short.

i: Hollin Strake, census officer, off duty
s: The Reader's Tag is a side quest, asked by Hollin Strake (census officer, off duty). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Hollin Strake: You found me. Good. I was afraid somebody else would first.

Hollin Strake: Word's going up and down the road that somebody opened the cells on Saint Orra's. That the beam's out. They told us the isle sorted people for service in the city. I read that off a card, too, for nine years.

Hollin Strake: I never went back after the reply sack. So they've done what they do. There's a tag post at the crossroads by the posting-house. My brother rode past it and wouldn't tell me what he saw.
Hollin Strake: I want to see it written. I've written it on enough other people.
You: I'll look at the post.
Hollin Strake: The crossroads by the posting-house. And there's a knight asking for me at the farms. Sir Aumery. He'll be near it.
1. Look for Hollin's name on the crossroads tag post
2. Stop Sir Aumery Gale, who's been sent to collect Hollin
3. Tell Hollin Strake what his tag says
Look for Hollin's name on the crossroads tag post
"Census tags nailed up the post like scales, the linen gone grey in the weather. One is new and white."
"Pinned through the same nail, a receipt with the seal: 'The above presented himself freely for service, being of sound mind.' Signed in a small neat hand, with long loops on the R."
You: Presented himself freely. They've written that he came quietly, before they've caught him.
Tell Hollin Strake what his tag says
Hollin Strake: Well? Am I on it?
You: You're on it. 'Officer, lapsed. Received.' And a receipt: you presented yourself freely, being of sound mind. The same hand as the replies.
Hollin Strake: ...Sound mind. First time they've been right about me.
You: Sir Aumery won't be asking at the farms any more.
Hollin Strake: I liked him. That's the trouble with all of it. I liked most of them.
Hollin Strake: Take my sword. Nine years and I never drew it once. That was the job - it never needed drawing.
Hollin Strake: I keep reading my tag in my head. Received. It's not a bad word, said kindly. Nobody ever said it kindly.
Hollin Strake: Nine years on the road and I never once asked where the boat went. I'm asking now. Everyone's asking now.
: The man who wrote 'volunteer' for Edrin is on a list himself now? ...Good. No. I don't know. Ask me later.
Light Held in the Spire is a side quest, asked by Wynne Ashdown (crystal-cutter). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Wynne Ashdown: Crystal remembers light. I don't mean a story. Cut a spire on the right plane, hold it to the sun, and you'll see a sky from before you were born. Just for a breath.
Wynne Ashdown: I cut lamps from the young spires. Nobody cuts the old one in the middle - my master wouldn't touch it. But it split in the frost, on a clean plane, and I looked.
Wynne Ashdown: I saw a table. Out in the open, on grass, where the Hollow Crown is now. Two at it, signing. One of them had a crown on.
Wynne Ashdown: I didn't look at the other one properly. I didn't want to. Will you? Then I'll know whether I'm mad.
You: I'll look into the spire.
Wynne Ashdown: The old one, in the middle. Hold your hand flat over the split till it warms. Then look. Then stop looking.
1. Look into the split in the old crystal spire
2. Bring Wynne Ashdown 2 obsidian to cut the old spire clean
Look into the split in the old crystal spire
"The split runs through the foot of the old spire like a pane of glass, a gold fleck caught deep in it. You hold your hand over it until it warms. The light inside begins to move."
"Grass, and a wide plain where the chasm should be. A table of plain wood. A man in a crown, young, with the face from every statue, writing his name in a book."
"Across from him, something sitting very still in the shape of a man, as if it had read about men. It does not sign. It presses its thumb to the page, and the page smokes."
"Behind them the ground has started to tilt. In a stone under the table, the hooked sign cut into the gateway below the strait."
You: The covenant. The king signed his name. The creditor left its thumb.
Bring Wynne Ashdown 2 obsidian to cut the old spire clean
Wynne Ashdown: You saw it. Don't tell me. I can see you saw it.
You: A king signing. Something with its thumb on the page. And the ground starting to tip, under them.
Wynne Ashdown: The ground tipping. That's the Hollow Crown being made. They signed, and the land fell in, and the city went up off the top of it.
Wynne Ashdown: Obsidian. Good. I'll cut the plane out thin as a fingernail and set it in a lamp. Anyone who wants to tell me the Preserver saved us can hold it to the sun first.
Wynne Ashdown: Have the first lamp I cut from the young spires this year. It's only got sunlight in it. Ordinary sunlight. I checked.
Wynne Ashdown: People come and hold it to the sun now. Most of them don't say anything. One old man laughed for a long time.
Wynne Ashdown: I sleep with the young lamps by the bed. They only remember mornings.
: A king signing his name, and the ground falling in for it. Of course it was paperwork. It was always paperwork.

Quest(68).t: A Name off a Salt Tin
s: A Name off a Salt Tin is a side quest, asked by Salt (came home from below). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Salt: Call me Salt. It was on a tin in the first kitchen I came to after the stair. It's a good plain word, and people need something to shout.

Salt: I came up with the others when the dark below went quiet. Most of them knew which way to walk. I didn't. The Archive had my name a long time, and when it let go, the name didn't come up with me.
Salt: I've two things left. A bell with a crack in its lip. And a well with a fish cut in the stone. I was small. I could see the fish because I was the right height.
Salt: A man at the last farm says there's a hamlet over the ridge with a cracked bell. Will you go first? If it's not the right one, I don't want to see it.
Salt: Over the ridge. Look at the frame. Children carve frames. I think I did.
1. Find the cracked bell in the hamlet over the ridge
2. Ask in the hamlet whose fish is carved on the bell-frame
3. Tell Salt whose name was on the bell-frame
Find the cracked bell in the hamlet over the ridge
"An old chapel bell on a frame, a crack running up from its lip. Not a census bell - smaller, rougher. A village bell."
"The frame is covered in children's carvings, generations deep. Initials. A dog. A boat. Low down, where a small child could reach: a fish."
"Beside the fish, in the same small hand: BEK. Under it, cut by an older hand, a row of notches - one a year, by the look of it - that goes on a long way, and then stops."
You: Bek. Somebody counted the years for her, until they couldn't.
Ask in the hamlet whose fish is carved on the bell-frame
They: You're looking at Bek's fish. Nobody looks at Bek's fish but me.
They: Bekka Tench. My aunt. Taken the year I was born, and that's eighty years. My mother cut a notch for her every spring till she died, and I cut them after, till my hands went.
You: She's alive. She's over the ridge. She calls herself Salt, because her name didn't come back with her.
They: ...She'll be young, won't she. They say it's like that, below. She'll be younger than me.
They: Tell her the well's still there. The fish is still there. Tell her she's Bekka, and she always cried when the bell rang, and her sister never once missed a spring.
Tell Salt whose name was on the bell-frame
You: A cracked bell. A fish on the frame, low down, and a name beside it. Bek. Bekka Tench.
Salt: ...Bekka. That's it. That's how it sounds when somebody's cross with you for being late in.
You: Your sister cut a notch for you every spring until she died. Her daughter's still there. She's eighty. She says the well's still there.
Salt: Eighty. My sister's girl is eighty.
Salt: I'll keep Salt, I think. For the time I was gone. But I'll answer to Bekka. Here - I carried it up the stair and I never knew why. Now I do.
Salt: Marigold and I sit at the well. She tells me who I was. I tell her what it was like. We both stop before the bad bits.
Salt: I'm Bekka at the well and Salt on the road. I think that's allowed.
: Coming home without your name. Mara. I'm Mara Venn. I'm going to say it a few times today, if nobody minds.

i: Hesper Lyle, came down a refuse chute, once
s: The Landing Fires is a side quest, asked by Hesper Lyle (came down a refuse chute, once). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Hesper Lyle: Twelve years ago I went down a refuse chute in a sack of bones from the Long Kitchen. Broke both legs on the midden at the bottom. Best day of my life.
Hesper Lyle: I was Thornbound before I went, and down here I stayed it, in my way. We keep people on the ground. Lanterns on hills. Old signals.

Hesper Lyle: The launch is coming down with the common folk on it. Bakers, porters. The landing grounds are lit for them. And word's come from Kesh's people: when the city's bell goes, douse the fires. Let them come down in the dark.
Hesper Lyle: I said yes. A month ago I'd have meant it. My sister's on that launch. Find the signal lantern on the bald hill and read me the orders. I need to hear them in someone else's voice.
Hesper Lyle: The bald hill, past the sheepfold. A thorn cut in the hood. Somebody'll be minding it.
1. Find the Thornbound signal lantern on the bald hill
2. Stop Wick Thorley, who's minding the fires for the Thornbound
3. Tell Hesper Lyle what the orders said
Find the Thornbound signal lantern on the bald hill
"A shuttered lantern on the hilltop, burning low, a thorn cut into its hood. Folded under its foot, a paper."
"'To the ground. When the city's bell goes for the launch, every landing fire to be doused. They built nothing below and they will learn nothing below. Let the dark have them. - K.'"
"Below, in another hand: a tally of fires, and against each one, the name of who's to put it out. HESPER LYLE - THIRD FIRE. Ticked."
You: A list. They've made a list.
Tell Hesper Lyle what the orders said
Hesper Lyle: What did it say?
You: 'Let the dark have them.' Signed K. And a list of who's to douse which fire. Your name's on it, ticked.
Hesper Lyle: A list. We were going to be better than them, and the first thing we did was make a list.
You: Thorley won't be dousing anything.
Hesper Lyle: Then the fires stay lit. Every one. I'll sit by mine myself, and if a baker comes down out of the sky into it, I'll hand her a blanket and say nothing clever.
Hesper Lyle: Take this. A spoon from the Long Kitchen - the only thing in that sack that wasn't bones. I've kept it twelve years for a day worth spending it on.
Hesper Lyle: My sister came down two fires east of mine. I didn't know her. She knew the legs.
Hesper Lyle: I've stopped being Thornbound. Turns out you can just stop. Nobody comes round with a receipt.
: Someone wanted the landing fires put out? On people coming down? ...I'd have sat by one too.
The Stub-Book is a side quest, asked by Hollin Strake (nobody's officer now). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Hollin Strake: No king. No census. I keep putting my hand to my hip for a sword I gave you.
Hollin Strake: When I walked out, I buried my stub-book. Every receipt has a stub - the copy for the coastal office. Nine years of them. Every name I wrote 'volunteer' beside.
Hollin Strake: I'm going round. Every house in that book, I knock, and I say what really happened. Some doors won't open. That's fair.
Hollin Strake: But there's one I can't knock on. Vale, Edrin. Briar's Rest. You know them. Dig up the book and take his stub to his sister. Please.
You: I'll take it to Nessa.
Hollin Strake: Under the third milestone from the posting-house. An arm deep, in oilcloth. I was always tidy.
1. Dig up Hollin's stub-book under the third milestone
2. Take Edrin's receipt stub to Nessa Vale
3. Tell Hollin Strake what Nessa said
Dig up Hollin's stub-book under the third milestone
"A stub-book wrapped in oilcloth, swollen at the edges. Hundreds of stubs, each a name, a place, a date, and VOLUNTEER in the same neat ink."
"One stub is folded down at the corner. VALE, EDRIN. BRIAR'S REST. VOLUNTEER."

"On the back, in newer ink and a different hand - bigger, shakier: 'He did not volunteer. He hit me in the mouth and said his sister would find him. I wrote it because the count had to come right. It was my hand that wrote it. H. Strake.'"
You: He's signed it. His own name, this time.
Take Edrin's receipt stub to Nessa Vale
You: A receipt stub. Edrin's. The officer who wrote it has put what really happened on the back, and signed it.
They: 'He hit me in the mouth and said his sister would find him.' That's Edrin. That's every word of him.
They: He's out in the yard splitting wood. I'm going to show him this, and he's going to laugh, and I'm going to let him.
They: Tell Strake I've read it. Tell him the count's come right now. Tell him not to come here. Not yet. Maybe at harvest.
Tell Hollin Strake what Nessa said
Hollin Strake: Did she read it?
You: She read it. Edrin laughed. She says the count's come right now. And not to come yet. Maybe at harvest.
Hollin Strake: That's the kindest thing anyone's said to me since the sky went empty.
Hollin Strake: Have my coat. It's oiled. It kept that book dry nine years, it'll keep you dry a few.
Hollin Strake: Two hundred and twelve doors. Forty-one opened. Six people hit me. I'd say it's going well.
Hollin Strake: I've started writing other things down. Weather. What people grow. Nobody needs it, which is the best thing about it.
: Edrin's nailed that stub over the door. Says it's the only true receipt the crown ever wrote. I told him the crown didn't write it.
: Edrin hit an officer in the mouth? I'm going to ask him to show me how.

i: Ambrose Thale, schoolmaster of the city, once
s: The Gazetteer of Ruins is a side quest, asked by Ambrose Thale (schoolmaster of the city, once). Givers turn up at inns, camps and villages as you travel, once the story is far enough along.
Ambrose Thale: I taught geography. A school on the Fourth Terrace, the children of clerks. I was considered very good.

Ambrose Thale: 'The Lower Provinces.' A ruin since the Reckoning, every mile of it. Plague, then famine, then the sea. The Preserver lifted the worthy and let the land below rest. I taught it thirty years. I drew the maps myself.
Ambrose Thale: I came down on the launch. I have walked for nine days through ruins that keep offering me soup.
Ambrose Thale: My schoolroom fell somewhere out there. The Gazetteer's in it - my own copy, with my notes. Bring me the page for this province. I want to read it standing in it.
Ambrose Thale: White plaster and a blue door, I should think. They were all white plaster and blue doors. Thank you. I'm told that's what people say here.
1. Find Ambrose Thale's fallen schoolroom and his Gazetteer
2. Bring Ambrose Thale the page from his Gazetteer
Find Ambrose Thale's fallen schoolroom and his Gazetteer
"A slab of white plaster with a blue-painted door still in it. Under it, a smashed bookcase, and schoolbooks swollen with dew."
"'THE LOWER PROVINCES. A ruin since the Reckoning. No inhabitants. The roads are lost and the wells are poisoned. Let the children of Crownreach give thanks that they need never go down.'"
"In the margin, in a teacher's careful pencil: 'Ask: who grows the grain for the Long Kitchen?' And under it, smaller: '(Do not ask this.)'"
You: He asked. Once. In pencil.
Bring Ambrose Thale the page from his Gazetteer
Ambrose Thale: My pencil. I'd forgotten I'd done that.
Ambrose Thale: 'No inhabitants. The wells are poisoned.' I've drunk from eleven wells. A woman at the last one charged me a turnip, and she was right to.
You: You wrote 'ask who grows the grain'. And then 'do not ask this'.
Ambrose Thale: A clerk's boy asked it once, in class. Bright boy. His family were moved to a lower terrace the next season. I wrote the note that night and never said it aloud again.

Ambrose Thale: I'm going to write a new one. The Lower Provinces, by someone who's walked them. It'll mostly be about soup. Take this - the only map in the school that was ever right. It's of the stars.
Ambrose Thale: Chapter one: the soup. Chapter two: the people who make the soup. I'm told there will be a great many chapters.
Ambrose Thale: Children here ask me what the city was like. I tell them it was very clean, and it was lying.
: There's a man who used to teach in the sky. He says the waterfalls never reached the ground. They went to mist on the way. I knew it. I knew it.

A soldier's journal (the watchtower) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).

Twelve received at dusk. Nine on the officer's paper. He told me to count the chains if numbers troubled me. One woman asked whether her son could see the city from the ship. I said yes because I could not think what else to say. No ship is listed for us tomorrow. We go to the coastal office.
Transport, east road. Taken on at the crossing: W. Marsh, of Fenn Ford. A. Coyle, of Fenn Ford. Next: Briar's Rest, the old waystation - census at the third bell, the
Royal notice (the toll booth) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).

BY COMMAND OF HIS MAJESTY ALDREN THE PRESERVER. Let every soul of this district be entered at the census bell. Tribute is the gratitude of the preserved; service is the privilege of the able. Whosoever conceals a person from the census conceals that person from His Majesty's protection.
The officer's list (Briar's Rest) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).

Census of Briar's Rest, the waystation, expanded by order. Goods: as tallied. Persons fit for service: Venn, Tomas, nineteen years. Previous receipts, this settlement: Vale, Edrin - received, volunteer; receipt issued. Carry forward the shortfall to the coastal office.
A torn tag (the convoy camp) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).
A strip of linen, stitched in black thread, torn across: VENN, T. - BRIAR'S - XIX. It was caught on a bar of the cage wagon.

Doc(\"A letter never sent (the Last Vein.t: A letter never sent (the Last Vein)
s: A letter never sent (the Last Vein) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).

There is worked stone under the seam, though nobody admits sending men this deep before us. The bell rang again while the lift was stopped. Renn heard his mother below the stair. His mother died in winter. We have barred the opening with the spare rails. Tell Oren I would rather owe him another set of tools than go back for these.
Register of passage (Three Toll Fort) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).
East road. Persons received under census this quarter: thirty-one. Forwarded to the receiving office, Saint Orra's Isle: thirty-one. Returned: wagons, six, empty.
Against every line, in the same hand: S.O. intake - acknowledged.

Doc(\"A guard's letter, never sent (Thre.t: A guard's letter, never sent (Three Toll Fort)
s: A guard's letter, never sent (Three Toll Fort) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).

Mother - I am well and fed and the roof keeps the rain off. Do not believe what they say about the road. More come down it in chains in a month than every ship to the city could carry in a year, and I have never seen one of those ships.
The wagons come back empty. They have us scrub the shackles before they go out again, so nobody sees what was on them. Nobody here asks where to. I asked once.
The corrected manifest (Ilyan's dispatch case) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).
Public return: thirty-six laborers delivered for royal service.
Private correction: twenty-eight to the island intake, six retained for examination, two deceased before acceptance. Remove the dead from the service total. Retain them in the obligation total.

Doc(\"Pilot report on unauthorized ascen.t: Pilot report on unauthorized ascent (the landing tower)
s: Pilot report on unauthorized ascent (the landing tower) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).
Lift sufficient. Frame sound. At the boundary, passenger lost grip without visible injury. Gold mark appeared at the throat. City engine turned toward us before the passenger could speak.
Armor did not delay the discharge. Permission precedes passage. Height does not alter permission.

Doc(\"The trial of Vaelis, witness copy.t: The trial of Vaelis, witness copy (the monastery)
s: The trial of Vaelis, witness copy (the monastery) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).
Official record: the accused, Vaelis, warden of the city's protection, charged with attempting to admit contaminated outsiders to the preserved city. The accused declined to answer.

Witness copy: They asked whether I had made a door for the unchosen. I answered that I had made a door for people. The clerk asked that the distinction be removed from the record. His Majesty did not look at me until I named the source beneath the throne. Then he dismissed the witnesses.
In the margin, another hand: He was trying to tell us where the king's protection comes from.
Sera Quill's tide charts (Reedwake) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).

Soundings for the strait, in Sera's hand, years of them. A cove under the isle's north cliff is circled twice: Dry at the spring ebb - two hours, no more. Watch tower sees it at the flood. Don't come at the flood.
A sister's note (the ruined chapel) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).
Four in the cistern tonight, and the boy with the cough. Sister Anwe brings bread at the low tide; the guards don't come down the old stair, the damp gets in their armour.
The Abbess dined with the inspector again. She says we keep the sanctuary by keeping the peace. She says the names will be safer in his books than in ours.
I have hidden the first register where the drowned are. If they find this, I wrote it alone. - M.

Doc(\"The first register of Saint Orra\".t: The first register of Saint Orra
s: The first register of Saint Orra is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).

Year 1 of the Reckoning. Received from the wreck of the Gull: seven living, two drowned, the drowned buried at the north stones and named. Received from the road: forty-one, without papers, kept at the sanctuary. Anwe Coyle, Tobin Marsh, Ede Rook, Wren of Fenn Ford, and more.
Year 9. Received by the crown's order: sixty. Kept at the sanctuary: sixty. Forwarded: none. The sisters will not forward.
Year 31, in another hand: The sanctuary keeps no names. By order of the inspector, with the consent of the Abbess.
Two manifests (the inspection chamber) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).
Crown copy, this quarter: Persons received for royal service: forty. Servants, twenty-two. Patients, under examination, eleven. Condemned, seven. Delivered.

The other copy, same forty names, in a hand that slants the wrong way: Twenty-two to the Furnace. Eleven to the Archive, to be read. Seven to the Bastion. Obligation renewed: forty. Tribute satisfied: the quarter.
Vaelis transfer order is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).

Deliver Vaelis intact to the Last Gaol. Preserve speech, memory, and hands. No execution is authorized. No substitution will be accepted. His Majesty's preference for silence does not supersede the creditor's claim upon useful knowledge.
Beneath it, a stack of the same order, renewed every year. The oldest is dated Year 18. The newest is dated this spring.
On the Counterseal (the inspector's study) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).

The king may close his gates to merchants, kin, and armies. He may not close them to inspection. The first impression remains with me. Do not confuse his enrolled subjects with the authority that permits their enrollment. Should he withhold tribute, I enter without his invitation.
The conduit ledger (the inspector's study) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).

For the successor to this office. The conduit above the spire carries passage and tribute between this office and the city's ward. Should the office fall vacant, the conduit fails, and with it every temporary passage.

The ward does not fail. It is not fastened to this office or to its holder's heart. It is bound to the instrument the signatory bears, and to his continuance. Do not trouble the creditor with fears for the ward while the king still breathes.
The intake ledger (the tally dais) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).
Received this quarter by the isle's stair: forty. Allocated: to the Furnace, twenty-two. To the Archive, eleven. To the Bastion, seven. Obligation renewed: forty.

Awaiting allocation, carried forward: Coyle, Anwe, of Fenn Ford, from the sanctuary of Saint Orra. Received Year 31. Will not answer to her name. Carried forward. Carried forward. Carried forward. (The same two words, one line a year, in the same hand, for two hundred and forty-seven years.)
Hollis, Davin, fourteen. Asks questions. To the Archive, to be read.
In the margin, struck through: Warder Brann - refused the Archive transfer. Removed from the roll. Held in the count room pending allocation.

Doc(\"Standing order of the March (the p.t: Standing order of the March (the patrol captain's belt)
s: Standing order of the March (the patrol captain's belt) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).

To the patrols of the March, under the Bastion's seal. Every route that reaches the Last Gaol is closed to all movement not under seal: the causeway, the river stairs, the chain roads. Any living thing on the March without a mark is to be received.

The captive Vaelis, taken from the River of Names after his attempt, is returned to the Gaol under its own seal and will be moved no further. His hands are to be kept. His speech is to be kept. He is not to be given ink.

Doc(\"Words on a prison wall (the canyon.t: Words on a prison wall (the canyon of the River of Names)
s: Words on a prison wall (the canyon of the River of Names) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).
I knew the name they called. It was mine. I knew the village too. What I did not know was that writing a child in a book could follow her here.
If you go back, tell them to stop bringing their babies to the census bell.
The three restraints (Ysra's notes) is one of the papers of the story. Read it where you find it (E) and it's kept in your journal (L).
Heat holds the work. A name holds the claim. Iron holds the body. None is enough alone.
The wizard has learned to loosen one, so they keep the other two taut. Find where each is fastened. Do not waste your strength on the bars they want you to strike.
Every claim is written twice. The king's clerks write the copy, in his mark the right way round. The creditor writes the original, in the same mark reversed. Copies are bait.
